Reduced Cost Influence Functions for Predict-then-Optimize under Noisy Data

William Zhang Affiliation: Operations Research Center Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology Affiliation: Cambridge, MA 02139 Email: wzhang64@mit.edu    Saurabh Amin Affiliation: Operations Research Center Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology Affiliation: Cambridge, MA 02139 Email: amins@mit.edu    Georgia Perakis Affiliation: Operations Research Center Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology Affiliation: Cambridge, MA 02139 Email: georgiap@mit.edu
Abstract

Machine learning models deployed in decision-making pipelines, from vehicle routing to dynamic pricing to clinical decision support, must remain reliable in the face of low-quality training data. We study a predict-then-optimize setting in which an upstream model predicts the cost vector of a downstream linear program, with a large pool of noisy training data supplemented by a small curated set of clean data. We introduce Reduced Cost Influence Functions (RCIFs), which combine influence functions from robust statistics with the geometry of linear optimization to estimate how each training point shifts downstream decisions. Building on this, we propose a reweighting algorithm that uses RCIFs to downweight harmful training points and reduce downstream regret. Experiments on random linear programs and shortest-path problems show that our approach reduces regret, and accompanying theory characterizes properties of RCIFs and identifies regimes favorable to our method relative to baselines.

1 Introduction

Machine learning models are increasingly used as components of larger decision-making pipelines: pricing engines, routing systems, clinical decision support tools. In these pipelines, predictions are not the end of the line: they are passed to a downstream optimization procedure whose solution carries the real consequences. This shift makes the training of predictive models a more delicate problem, since small errors under standard prediction loss can produce suboptimal downstream decisions. Compounding this, machine learning models are well known to be vulnerable to low-quality training data (Biggio and Roli, 2018), and a decision pipeline that is brittle to training-time corruption can produce costly errors downstream. Thus, how can we improve robustness of the downstream decision against corrupted training data via the upstream training process?

We propose a downstream-aware reweighting of the training data that leaves both the predictor architecture and the downstream optimization method unchanged. Our method assumes access to a small clean validation set, a standard assumption in robust learning literature (Ren et al., 2018; Hendrycks et al., 2018), in addition to a larger, potentially corrupted training set. We introduce the core technical object, the reduced cost influence function (RCIF), a decision-aware signal that propagates the effect of upweighting each training point through the upstream predictor onto the reduced costs of the downstream LP, directly connecting each training point to the outcome decision. The RCIF measures how each training point destabilizes or stabilizes the downstream decision boundary; we use it to reweight the training data using the validation set, so that the refit predictor produces decisions that are robust to training corruption.

Our method is best suited to predict-then-optimize problems in which (i) prediction errors frequently cause decision flips, (ii) training data is corrupted, and (iii) a small clean validation set exists but is too small to fit the predictor on its own. We demonstrate gains on random linear programs and on shortest-path routing, a standard benchmark for decision-making pipelines (Elmachtoub and Grigas, 2022), and provide theoretical guarantees identifying validation-size regimes favorable to RCIF reweighting relative to both the standard, unweighted estimator and validation-only estimator.

2 Related Work

Decision-aware learning.

A large body of work studies training predictive models for downstream tasks. End-to-end approaches train the upstream predictor with respect to downstream decision quality, most notably via surrogate losses such as SPO+ (Elmachtoub and Grigas, 2022) and the broader decision-aware learning literature (Hu et al., 2022; Shah et al., 2022; Qi et al., 2025; Donti et al., 2017; Bertsimas and Kallus, 2020). Our approach is complementary: rather than modifying the training loss, we reweight the training data using a downstream-aware signal, leaving both the predictor and the LP unchanged. This is similar to Lawless and Zhou (2022), which directly reweights data via regret but does not consider corrupted data.

Robustness in decision-aware learning.

A parallel line of work addresses robustness in decision-aware learning. Work such as Sun et al. (2023); Yeh et al. (2024); Patel et al. (2024) consider robustness via sharper uncertainty sets using conformal prediction, while Schutte et al. (2023); Im et al. (2025) propose surrogate losses for robust decision-focused learning. Instead, we directly reweight the training data, which preserves the original pipeline and focuses on robustness to the training phase rather than at deployment via robust downstreams.

Reweighting under noisy data.

Mitigating label corruption given access to a small clean set (and reweighting data) is prevalent in robust learning (Hendrycks et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021). Other work considers corruption detection such as (Northcutt et al., 2021; Diakonikolas et al., 2019; Sheikholeslami et al., 2021). Notably, Ren et al. (2018) derive weights from influence functions (popularized in (Koh and Liang, 2017; Broderick et al., 2020)) for robustness. We adopt the influence-function machinery but propagate effects onto reduced costs of the downstream LP rather than onto prediction loss, which differentiates our approach from a direct adaptation of validation-loss influence.

3 Setting

We consider a predict-then-optimize pipeline in which an upstream predictive model produces an estimate of an unknown cost vector, which is then passed to a downstream linear program whose solution is the final decision.

Downstream optimization.

The downstream component solves a linear program of the form

x∗​(c)=arg​minx∈𝒳⁡c⊤​x,x^{*}(c)=\argmin_{x\in\mathcal{X}}c^{\top}x,

where c∈ℝdc\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the cost vector and 𝒳={x∈ℝd:Ax=b,x≥0}\mathcal{X}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:Ax=b,\,x\geq 0\} is a closed, bounded polyhedron with diameter LL defined by a constraint matrix A∈ℝa×dA\in\mathbb{R}^{a\times d} and a right-hand side b∈ℝab\in\mathbb{R}^{a}. We assume throughout that the LP is nondegenerate, so that each optimal vertex corresponds to a unique basis.

Upstream predictor and data.

The upstream component is a regression model fθ:𝒵→ℝdf_{\theta}:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} mapping features z∈𝒵⊆ℝqz\in\mathcal{Z}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{q} to predicted cost vectors, parameterized by θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta with true parameter θ⋆∈Θ\theta^{\star}\in\Theta. We have access to two datasets: training data 𝒮={(zi,c~i)}i=1n\mathcal{S}=\{(z_{i},\tilde{c}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} with possibly corrupted labels, and clean validation data 𝒱={(zv,cv)}v=1m\mathcal{V}=\{(z_{v},c_{v})\}_{v=1}^{m} with uncorrupted labels, where typically m≪nm\ll n.

The label model is

ci=fθ⋆​(zi)+εi,c_{i}\;=\;f_{\theta^{\star}}(z_{i})+\varepsilon_{i},

with εi\varepsilon_{i} zero-mean σε\sigma_{\varepsilon}-subgaussian and mutually independent. A subset 𝒞⊆{1,…,n}\mathcal{C}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\} of size |𝒞|=β​n|\mathcal{C}|=\beta n, β∈(0,1/2)\beta\in(0,1/2), indexes the corrupted training points:

c~i=ci+ηi(i∈𝒞),c~i=ci(i∉𝒞),\tilde{c}_{i}\;=\;c_{i}+\eta_{i}\quad(i\in\mathcal{C}),\qquad\tilde{c}_{i}\;=\;c_{i}\quad(i\notin\mathcal{C}),

where ηi\eta_{i} is an additional perturbation. The validation set 𝒱\mathcal{V} contains the clean costs cjc_{j} by assumption. Throughout the paper, c~i\tilde{c}_{i} denotes the observed training label at index ii, which equals the clean label cic_{i} when i∉𝒞i\notin\mathcal{C}. Equivalently, ηi=0\eta_{i}=0 for i∉𝒞i\notin\mathcal{C}, so the decomposition c~i=ci+ηi\tilde{c}_{i}=c_{i}+\eta_{i} holds for all ii.

Fitting algorithm.

Given a loss function ℓ:ℝd×ℝd→ℝ\ell:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}, the standard empirical risk minimizer (ERM) on the training data is

θ^=arg​minθ∈Θ∑i=1nℓ(fθ(zi),c~i).\hat{\theta}=\argmin_{\theta\in\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell(f_{\theta}(z_{i}),\tilde{c}_{i}).

For a given set of weights p1,…,pnp_{1},\dots,p_{n}, one can instead obtain the weighted ERM

θ^p=arg​minθ∈Θ∑i=1npiℓ(fθ(zi),c~i),\hat{\theta}_{p}=\argmin_{\theta\in\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\,\ell(f_{\theta}(z_{i}),\tilde{c}_{i}),

with larger weights placing greater emphasis on the ii-th training point. We assume throughout that the empirical risk is strictly convex in θ\theta and twice differentiable (Koh and Liang, 2017), so that influence-function approximations are well defined.

4 Preliminaries

Bases, reduced costs, and optimality cones.

A basis B⊆{1,…,d}B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\} is a set of indices such that the submatrix ABA_{B} is invertible and AB−1​b≥0A_{B}^{-1}b\geq 0 is feasible, and N⁡(B)={1,…,d}∖BN(B)=\{1,\ldots,d\}\setminus B denotes the corresponding nonbasic set. For each nonbasic index k∈N⁡(B)k\in N(B), the edge direction is a dd-dimensional vector

δ⁡(B,k)=[−AB−1​Akek],\delta(B,k)=\begin{bmatrix}-A_{B}^{-1}A_{k}\\ e_{k}\end{bmatrix},

where eke_{k} is the elementary unit vector in nonbasic coordinates corresponding to nonbasic index kk. The edge direction represents the direction along which the nonbasic variable xkx_{k} can increase from zero while maintaining feasibility (Bennouna et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026). The reduced cost of nonbasic variable kk under cost vector cc and basis BB is

sk​(c,B)=c⊤​δ​(B,k),s_{k}(c,B)=c^{\top}\delta(B,k),

and BB is optimal for cc if and only if sk​(c,B)≥0s_{k}(c,B)\geq 0 for all k∈N⁡(B)k\in N(B). The set of cost vectors for which BB is optimal forms the optimality cone

Λ(B)={c∈ℝd:sk(c,B)≥0 for all k∈N(B)},\Lambda(B)=\{c\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:s_{k}(c,B)\geq 0\text{ for all }k\in N(B)\},

and the cones {Λ⁡(B)}B\{\Lambda(B)\}_{B} cover ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with overlaps only on measure-zero boundaries. Two cost vectors in the same cone induce the same optimal decision.

Regret.

The quality of a predicted cost vector c^\hat{c} relative to the true cost cc is measured by the downstream regret:

Regret⁡(c^,c)=c⊤​x∗​(c^)−c⊤​x∗​(c),\mathrm{Regret}(\hat{c},c)=c^{\top}x^{*}(\hat{c})-c^{\top}x^{*}(c),

the excess true cost incurred by acting optimally under c^\hat{c} rather than cc. Regret is zero whenever c^\hat{c} and cc lie in the same optimality cone, regardless of error ‖c^−c‖\|\hat{c}-c\|.

Influence functions.

Influence functions (Koh and Liang, 2017) provide a first-order approximation to the effect of perturbing the training distribution on the learned parameters. Consider the estimator obtained by upweighting training point wj=(zj,c~j)w_{j}=(z_{j},\tilde{c}_{j}) by ϵ\epsilon:

θ^ϵ,wj=arg​minθ⁡1n​∑i=1nℓ⁡(fθ​(zi),c~i)+ϵ​ℓ​(fθ​(zj),c~j).\hat{\theta}_{\epsilon,w_{j}}=\argmin_{\theta}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell(f_{\theta}(z_{i}),\tilde{c}_{i})+\epsilon\,\ell(f_{\theta}(z_{j}),\tilde{c}_{j}).

Under our risk assumptions, the derivative of θ^ϵ,wj\hat{\theta}_{\epsilon,w_{j}} with respect to ϵ\epsilon at ϵ=0\epsilon=0 admits the closed form

ℐθ^​(wj):=d​θ^ϵ,wjd​ϵ|ϵ=0=−Hθ^−1​∇θℓ​(fθ^​(zj),c~j),\mathcal{I}_{\hat{\theta}}(w_{j}):=\left.\frac{d\hat{\theta}_{\epsilon,w_{j}}}{d\epsilon}\right|_{\epsilon=0}=-H_{\hat{\theta}}^{-1}\nabla_{\theta}\ell(f_{\hat{\theta}}(z_{j}),\tilde{c}_{j}),

where Hθ^=1n​∑i=1n∇θ2ℓ​(fθ^​(zi),c~i)H_{\hat{\theta}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\nabla_{\theta}^{2}\ell(f_{\hat{\theta}}(z_{i}),\tilde{c}_{i}) is the empirical Hessian of the training loss at θ^\hat{\theta}. We refer to ℐθ^​(wj)\mathcal{I}_{\hat{\theta}}(w_{j}) as the influence of training point wjw_{j} on θ^\hat{\theta}.

5 Reduced cost influence function

Recall that downstream regret is zero whenever the predicted cost c^\hat{c} and the true cost cc lie in the same optimality cone. Thus the prediction need not be accurate in norm; it need only lie in the correct cone. Conversely, predictions near the boundary of Λ⁡(B)\Lambda(B) are unstable: small perturbations of c^\hat{c} can push the prediction into an adjacent cone and induce a discontinuous jump in downstream cost.

The reduced cost sk​(c,B)s_{k}(c,B) measures the slack in the kk-th constraint defining Λ⁡(B)\Lambda(B). Geometrically, the distance from cc to the kk-th cone boundary equals sk​(c,B)/‖δ⁡(B,k)‖s_{k}(c,B)/\|\delta(B,k)\|, and the overall margin is given by the minimum such distance over k∈N⁡(B)k\in N(B) (this margin coincides with distance to degeneracy (El Balghiti et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2023) under nondegeneracy). Our goal is to quantify the influence of each training point on this margin, identify harmful points (particularly in 𝒞\mathcal{C}), and downweight them. To this end we introduce reduced cost influence functions (RCIFs).

Fix a validation input zv∈𝒱z_{v}\in\mathcal{V} and let c^v=fθ^​(zv)\hat{c}_{v}=f_{\hat{\theta}}(z_{v}) be the predicted cost at zvz_{v}. Let BB be the optimal basis for c^v\hat{c}_{v}, and let k∈N⁡(B)k\in N(B) be a nonbasic index of interest. We wish to quantify how upweighting training point wjw_{j} changes the reduced cost sk​(c^v,B)s_{k}(\hat{c}_{v},B) at the validation point zvz_{v}.

Viewing sks_{k} as a function of θ\theta through the predictor, we have sk​(fθ​(zv),B)=δ​(B,k)⊤​fθ​(zv)s_{k}(f_{\theta}(z_{v}),B)=\delta(B,k)^{\top}f_{\theta}(z_{v}). Applying the chain rule and evaluating at θ=θ^\theta=\hat{\theta} in the influence direction ℐθ^​(wj)\mathcal{I}_{\hat{\theta}}(w_{j}) yields the following definition.

Definition 1 (Reduced Cost Influence Function).

Let θ^\hat{\theta} be the ERM hypothesis, let zvz_{v} be a validation input, let c^v=fθ^​(zv)\hat{c}_{v}=f_{\hat{\theta}}(z_{v}), and let BB be the optimal basis for c^v\hat{c}_{v}. For a nonbasic index k∈N⁡(B)k\in N(B) and a training point wjw_{j}, the reduced cost influence function is

RCIFk,θ^​(zv,wj):=δ​(B,k)⊤​∇θfθ^​(zv)​ℐθ^​(wj).\mathrm{RCIF}_{k,\hat{\theta}}(z_{v},w_{j}):=\delta(B,k)^{\top}\,\nabla_{\theta}f_{\hat{\theta}}(z_{v})\,\mathcal{I}_{\hat{\theta}}(w_{j}).

The RCIF admits a direct interpretation: it is the first-order approximation of the change in the reduced cost sk​(c^v,B)s_{k}(\hat{c}_{v},B) at validation point zvz_{v} when training point wjw_{j} is upweighted by a unit of ϵ\epsilon. A positive RCIF means upweighting wjw_{j} increases the reduced cost in direction kk, pushing c^v\hat{c}_{v} deeper into Λ⁡(B)\Lambda(B) along that facet. This signed, direction-aware signal is the basis for the reweighting schemes introduced in the next section.

5.1 RCIF score

We use the RCIF to construct aggregate scores for reweighting and refitting the predictor. We present two score variants: a natural two-sided score and a second, more refined directed score.

5.1.1 Two-sided weighting scheme

For each validation point wv∈𝒱w_{v}\in\mathcal{V}, let c^v=fθ^​(zv)\hat{c}_{v}=f_{\hat{\theta}}(z_{v}) be the predicted cost, BvB_{v} the optimal basis for c^v\hat{c}_{v}, and define the most fragile nonbasic direction as

kv∗=arg​mink∈N⁡(Bv)⁡sk​(c^v,Bv)‖δ⁡(Bv,k)‖,k^{*}_{v}=\argmin_{k\in N(B_{v})}\frac{s_{k}(\hat{c}_{v},B_{v})}{\left\lVert\delta(B_{v},k)\right\rVert},

i.e., the nonbasic index with the smallest reduced cost margin under c^v\hat{c}_{v}. This is the direction along which c^v\hat{c}_{v} is closest to the boundary of Λ⁡(Bv)\Lambda(B_{v}), and thus the direction most vulnerable to a basis flip.

We say validation point wvw_{v} is correct if BvB_{v} is also the optimal basis under the true cost cvc_{v}, i.e., if c^v\hat{c}_{v} and cvc_{v} lie in the same optimality cone, and incorrect otherwise. Let σv=2⋅𝟏correct​(wv)−1∈{−1,+1}\sigma_{v}=2\cdot\mathbf{1}_{\text{correct}}(w_{v})-1\in\{-1,+1\} encode this status.

The two-sided aggregate score for training point wjw_{j} is

ΨjTS=1m​∑wv∈𝒱σv⋅RCIFkv∗,θ^​(zv,wj).\Psi_{j}^{\text{TS}}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{w_{v}\in\mathcal{V}}\sigma_{v}\cdot\mathrm{RCIF}_{k^{*}_{v},\hat{\theta}}(z_{v},w_{j}).

The sign σv\sigma_{v} aligns two cases: at correct validation points we want to push c^v\hat{c}_{v} deeper into Λ⁡(Bv)\Lambda(B_{v}), and at incorrect points, we wish to destabilize the current basis so that c^v\hat{c}_{v} may exit the wrong cone.

5.1.2 Directed weighting scheme

The two-sided score destabilizes incorrect validation points along the direction of smallest current margin, but this direction is not necessarily the one that would move c^v\hat{c}_{v} toward the correct cone. We have access to the true cost cvc_{v} and can identify the directions along which the true cvc_{v} indicates a basis change is warranted: specifically, those nonbasic indices k∈N⁡(Bv)k\in N(B_{v}) for which sk​(cv,Bv)<0s_{k}(c_{v},B_{v})<0. These are the directions in which the true cost violates the optimality condition of the current basis BvB_{v}, and hence the directions whose nonbasic variables should enter the basis under cvc_{v}.

We refine the choice of kv∗k^{*}_{v} accordingly. For correct validation points, we keep the most fragile direction as before. For incorrect validation points, we restrict the argmin to the set of true-cost-violating directions:

k∗v={arg​mink∈N⁡(Bv)⁡sk​(c^v,Bv)‖δ⁡(Bv,k)‖,if ​v​ is correct,arg​mink∈N⁡(Bv):sk​(cv,Bv)<0sk​(c^v,Bv)‖δ⁡(Bv,k)‖,if ​v​ is incorrect.k^{*}_{v}=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\argmin_{k\in N(B_{v})}\frac{s_{k}(\hat{c}_{v},B_{v})}{\left\lVert\delta(B_{v},k)\right\rVert},&\text{if }v\text{ is correct,}\\[6.45831pt] \displaystyle\argmin_{k\in N(B_{v})\,:\,s_{k}(c_{v},B_{v})<0}\frac{s_{k}(\hat{c}_{v},B_{v})}{\left\lVert\delta(B_{v},k)\right\rVert},&\text{if }v\text{ is incorrect.}\end{cases}

The directed aggregate score uses the same outer formula as the two-sided score but with this refined choice of kv∗k^{*}_{v}:

ΨjD=1m​∑wv∈𝒱σv⋅RCIFkv∗,θ^​(zv,wj).\Psi^{\text{D}}_{j}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{w_{v}\in\mathcal{V}}\sigma_{v}\cdot\mathrm{RCIF}_{k^{*}_{v},\hat{\theta}}(z_{v},w_{j}).

The sign convention is unchanged. The refinement only changes which direction is destabilized. These scores can be used as additive weight adjustments directly, but an exponential refinement can improve performance in practice.

5.2 Exponential reweighting

Given an aggregate score Ψj\Psi_{j} (either ΨjTS\Psi_{j}^{\text{TS}} or ΨjD\Psi_{j}^{\text{D}}) for each training point, we convert scores to training weights via an exponential family with temperature parameter λ>0\lambda>0:

pj=exp⁡(λ​Ψj)∑i=1nexp⁡(λ​Ψi).p_{j}=\frac{\exp(\lambda\Psi_{j})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\exp(\lambda\Psi_{i})}.

We then refit the predictor by solving the weighted ERM problem with weights {pj}\{p_{j}\}. The temperature hyperparameter λ\lambda controls the aggressiveness of the reweighting: λ=0\lambda=0 recovers uniform weighting, while large λ\lambda concentrates mass on the highest-scoring training points. For experiments, we set λ=0.05\lambda=0.05.

5.3 Iterative reweighting

A single round of RCIF reweighting evaluates the influence of each training point at the original ERM estimator θ^\hat{\theta}. After the refit, however, the predictor has changed, and so have the optimal bases at validation points and the most fragile (or directed) nonbasic directions. We can sharpen the signal by recomputing the scores at the refitted estimator and accumulating them across iterations.

For τ\tau iterations, let Ψj(t)\Psi_{j}^{(t)} denote the aggregate score of training point wjw_{j} at the tt-th iteration, computed using θ^(t)\hat{\theta}^{(t)}, the predictor fitted at the start of iteration tt (with θ^(1)\hat{\theta}^{(1)} as unweighted ERM estimator). The iterative weight for wjw_{j} at iteration τ\tau is

pj(τ)=exp⁡(λ​∑t=1τΨj(t))∑i=1nexp⁡(λ​∑t=1τΨi(t)).p_{j}^{(\tau)}=\frac{\exp\left(\lambda\sum_{t=1}^{\tau}\Psi_{j}^{(t)}\right)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\exp\left(\lambda\sum_{t=1}^{\tau}\Psi_{i}^{(t)}\right)}.

Each iteration refits the predictor with weights pj(τ)p_{j}^{(\tau)}. We treat τ\tau as a hyperparameter; in our experiments we set τ=5\tau=5.

6 Theoretical results

We derive two properties of RCIF reweighting after one iteration of exponential weights: a signed score decrease for corrupted points, and validation-size regimes in which RCIF reweighting admits tighter regret upper bounds than the unweighted ERM and validation-only ERM baselines.

6.1 Setting and assumptions

We consider the same predict-then-optimize setting as defined in Section 3, but with a linear upstream model such that for parameter θ∈ℝd×q\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times q}, z∈ℛqz\in\mathcal{R}^{q}, fθ​(z)=θ​zf_{\theta}(z)=\theta z, and the loss function is square loss ℓ⁡(c,c^)=‖c−c^‖2\ell(c,\hat{c})=\|c-\hat{c}\|^{2}. Let θ^\hat{\theta} denote standard ERM on training set 𝒮\mathcal{S}, θ^p\hat{\theta}_{p} denote the one-step RCIF-reweighted ERM, and θ^val\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{val}} denote the validation-only ERM fit on 𝒱\mathcal{V}. Unless stated otherwise, throughout this section, we make the following assumptions.

(D1)

Bounded Features. Training and validation points (z,c)(z,c) are drawn iid from distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D}, with ‖z‖≤R\|z\|\leq R. Also let empirical design covariance Σ^:=1n​∑i=1nzi​zi⊤∈ℝq×q\hat{\Sigma}:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}z_{i}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times q} be invertible and satisfy λmineig​(Σ^)≥μ>0\lambda_{\min}^{\mathrm{eig}}(\hat{\Sigma})\geq\mu>0.

(D2)

Labels and noise. For both training and validation, for any ii, for true parameter θ∗\theta^{*}, ci=θ⋆​zi+εic_{i}=\theta^{\star}z_{i}+\varepsilon_{i} with each entry of εi\varepsilon_{i} 0-mean σε\sigma_{\varepsilon}-sub-Gaussian, independent of each other and features.

(D3)

Corruption set. A set 𝒞⊂{1,…,n}\mathcal{C}\subset\{1,\ldots,n\} of size |𝒞|=β​n|\mathcal{C}|=\beta n is drawn uniformly at random, independently of features and noise, with β∈(0,1/2)\beta\in(0,1/2).

(D4)

Bounded directional corruption. For j∈𝒞j\in\mathcal{C}, the corruption is of the form c~j=cj+ηj\tilde{c}_{j}=c_{j}+\eta_{j} where ηj=−α​δ^j\eta_{j}=-\alpha\,\hat{\delta}_{j}, and where δ^j:=δ⁡(Bj⋆,kj)/‖δ⁡(Bj⋆,kj)‖\hat{\delta}_{j}:=\delta(B_{j}^{\star},k_{j})/\|\delta(B_{j}^{\star},k_{j})\| is the unit-norm direction at the optimal basis Bj⋆B_{j}^{\star} at cjc_{j} for non-basic direction kj∈N⁡(Bj⋆)k_{j}\in N(B_{j}^{\star}) chosen independently of validation sample or learned estimator.

(D5)

Bounded LP geometry. ‖δ⁡(B,k)‖≤D\|\delta(B,k)\|\leq D for every basis BB and nonbasic kk.

6.2 RCIF score decomposition

We present a factorization of the RCIF, which leads to a score decomposition that isolates a “clean" RCIF score and a “corrupted" RCIF score from corruption ηj\eta_{j}.

Lemma 1 (RCIF Score Factorization).

We can factor the RCIF of training point wjw_{j} on a single validation input zvz_{v} on non-basic direction kk into two different terms, a downstream residual interaction term, and an input alignment term. Then we have that

RCIFk,θ^(zv,wj)=−δ​(Bv,k)⊤​rj⏟residual interaction⋅κ⁡(zv,zj)⏟input alignment\displaystyle\mathrm{RCIF}_{k,\hat{\theta}}(z_{v},w_{j})=-\underbrace{\delta(B_{v},k)^{\top}r_{j}}_{\textsc{residual interaction}}\cdot\underbrace{\kappa(z_{v},z_{j})}_{\textsc{input alignment}}

where κ⁡(zv,zj)\kappa(z_{v},z_{j}) denotes Mahalanobis inner product zvT​Σ^−1​zjz_{v}^{T}\hat{\Sigma}^{-1}z_{j} and rjr_{j} denotes the residual of training point jj, rj≔θ^​zj−c~jr_{j}\coloneqq\hat{\theta}z_{j}-\tilde{c}_{j}.

Now we may show that the RCIF score can be decomposed into a clean and corrupted term.

Lemma 2 (RCIF Score Decomposition).

For fixed θ^\hat{\theta} and training point wj=(zj,c~j)=(zj,cj+ηj)w_{j}=(z_{j},\tilde{c}_{j})=(z_{j},c_{j}+\eta_{j}), we can decompose the RCIF score Ψj\Psi_{j} into a clean score and noise term: Ψj=Ψjclean+uj⊤​ηj\Psi_{j}=\Psi_{j}^{\mathrm{clean}}+u_{j}^{\top}\eta_{j} where uj=1m​∑wv∈Vσv​κ​(zj,zv)​δ​(Bv,kv∗)u_{j}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{w_{v}\in V}\sigma_{v}\,\kappa(z_{j},z_{v})\delta(B_{v},k^{*}_{v}), where k∗k^{*} is the appropriate direction depending on the weighting scheme, and Ψjclean\Psi_{j}^{\mathrm{clean}} is the score if the score were calculated using wj=(zj,cj)w_{j}=(z_{j},c_{j}).

These lemmas hold without Assumptions (D1)-(D5) (handling any ηj\eta_{j}, not just the one in D4). Via this decomposition, we can obtain results that show how scoring on corrupted points differs between clean and corrupted points, with differences in magnitude under zero-mean corruption (see Appendix A.3) as well as signed score decrease for directional corruption as in D4.

6.3 Decreased corruption score

We show that under certain settings, our scoring method will give a lower score to corrupted points. First we define an alignment parameter.

Definition 2 (Validation alignment).

For a fresh sample (zj,cj)(z_{j},c_{j}), and fixed θ^\hat{\theta}, conditional on (θ^,zj,cj)(\hat{\theta},z_{j},c_{j}), define the alignment parameter

γ(θ^,zj,cj)≔𝔼wv∼𝒟[σvκ(zj,zv)δ(Bv,kv∗)⊤δ^j|θ^,zj,cj].\gamma(\hat{\theta},z_{j},c_{j})\;\coloneqq\;\mathbb{E}_{w_{v}\sim\mathcal{D}}\!\left[\sigma_{v}\kappa(z_{j},z_{v})\delta(B_{v},k^{*}_{v})^{\top}\hat{\delta}_{j}\,\middle|\,\hat{\theta},z_{j},c_{j}\right].
Theorem 1 (Signed score decrease under alignment; informal).

Adopt Assumptions (D1)–(D5). Let (zj,cj)(z_{j},c_{j}) be a fresh sample drawn from 𝒟\mathcal{D} independently of θ^\hat{\theta} and 𝒱\mathcal{V}, and let c~j=cj+ηj\tilde{c}_{j}=c_{j}+\eta_{j} be its directional corruption (D4). Suppose γ:=γ⁡(θ^,zj,cj)>0\gamma:=\gamma(\hat{\theta},z_{j},c_{j})>0. Then, in expectation over 𝒱\mathcal{V} conditional on (θ^,zj,cj)(\hat{\theta},z_{j},c_{j}), the score on the corrupted point is shifted by −α​γ-\alpha\gamma relative to its clean counterpart, and with probability at least 1−exp(−mγ2/(8Mγ2))1-\exp(-m\gamma^{2}/(8M_{\gamma}^{2})) over the same randomness, for constant MγM_{\gamma},

Ψj​(c~j)−Ψj​(cj)≤−α​γ2.\Psi_{j}(\tilde{c}_{j})-\Psi_{j}(c_{j})\;\leq\;-\frac{\alpha\gamma}{2}.

The full statement, constants, and proof appear as Theorem 4 in Appendix A.4.

Remark 1.

The assumption that γ>0\gamma>0 is a natural one. Note that σv>0\sigma_{v}>0 holds if θ^\hat{\theta} is similar to θ∗\theta^{*}, i.e. the upstream model makes predictions in the same cone. Furthermore, κ⁡(zv,zj)>0\kappa(z_{v},z_{j})>0 is likely positive if the distribution is tight around z¯=𝔼⁡[z]≠0\bar{z}=\mathbb{E}[z]\neq 0, with large nn. A tight distribution also makes δ​(Bv,kv∗)⊤​δ^j>0\delta(B_{v},k^{*}_{v})^{\top}\hat{\delta}_{j}>0 likely, as it holds when a large proportion of the cost-vector validation distribution falls into a single optimality cone with the same fragile direction.

Thus, if a freshly sampled point is corrupted via Assumption D4, w.h.p. its RCIF score is decreased compared to its clean counterpart. This requires the point to be out-of-sample, but we show an in-sample counterpart with an additional O⁡(1/n)O(1/n) slack in Appendix A.5.

6.4 Expected regret upper-bound comparison

Under further assumptions, we can obtain regimes on validation set size mm in which the RCIF reweighted solution θ^p\hat{\theta}_{p}, has tighter upper-bounds on the expected regret than those of the standard ERM solution θ^\hat{\theta}, and the validation-only solution θ^val\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{val}}. For intuition, we include two relevant assumptions below.

Assumption 1 (High probability alignment).

There exist constants γ0>0\gamma_{0}>0 and δγ∈(0,1/n)\delta_{\gamma}\in(0,1/n) such that

Pr[γ(θ^,zj,cj)≥γ0]≥ 1−δγ,\Pr\bigl[\gamma(\hat{\theta},z_{j},c_{j})\geq\gamma_{0}\bigr]\;\geq\;1-\delta_{\gamma},

where the probability is over (θ^,zj,cj)(\hat{\theta},z_{j},c_{j}) with θ^\hat{\theta} fit on iid samples drawn from 𝒟\mathcal{D} (D1) and (zj,cj)(z_{j},c_{j}) independently drawn from 𝒟\mathcal{D}.

The assumption says the conditional alignment is bounded away from zero with high probability. To obtain a result on regret, we require the following condition. Furthermore, let MM be an RCIF score upper-bound |Ψj|≤M|\Psi_{j}|\leq M, which holds under (D1)-(D5) with bounded residuals.

Assumption 2 (Margin).

There exists a constant ω>0\omega>0 such that

πv​(θ⋆​z)≥ 1/ωalmost surely under ​w=(z,c)∼𝒟,\pi_{v}(\theta^{\star}z)\;\geq\;1/\omega\quad\text{almost surely under }w=(z,c)\sim\mathcal{D},

where πv​(c):=mink∈N​(B⋆​(c))⁡sk​(c,B⋆​(c))/‖δ⁡(B⋆​(c),k)‖\pi_{v}(c):=\min_{k\in N(B^{\star}(c))}s_{k}(c,B^{\star}(c))/\|\delta(B^{\star}(c),k)\| is the reduced-cost margin at cc.

Theorem 2 (Validation-size regret regimes; informal).

Adopt Assumptions (D1)–(D5), Assumption 1, and Assumption 2, and additional regularity assumptions listed in Appendix  A.6. There exist thresholds m⋆​(λ),m⋆​(λ)∈[1,∞]m_{\star}(\lambda),m^{\star}(\lambda)\in[1,\infty], depending on the problem constants (e.g., σε,α,β,R,μ,D,γ0,ω\sigma_{\varepsilon},\alpha,\beta,R,\mu,D,\gamma_{0},\omega), such that in the asymptotic regime n→∞n\to\infty:

  1. 1.

    (Lower threshold m⋆m_{\star}.) For all m>m⋆​(λ)m>m_{\star}(\lambda), the RCIF reweighted estimator θ^p\hat{\theta}_{p} admits a tighter expected regret upper bound than the unweighted ERM θ^\hat{\theta}. The threshold is finite whenever the contraction factor Φ⁡(λ,m,n)\Phi(\lambda,m,n) from Lemma 6 eventually drops below β⋅A\beta\cdot A (for some constant AA) in mm.

  2. 2.

    (Upper threshold m⋆m^{\star}.) For all m<m⋆​(λ)m<m^{\star}(\lambda), θ^p\hat{\theta}_{p} admits a tighter expected regret upper bound than the validation-only ERM θ^val\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{val}}. The threshold is finite, since the irreducible corruption bias of θ^p\hat{\theta}_{p} eventually exceeds val-only’s 1/m1/m variance.

  3. 3.

    (Sweet spot.) When m⋆​(λ)<m⋆​(λ)m_{\star}(\lambda)<m^{\star}(\lambda), every mm in this interval admits a tighter expected regret upper bound for θ^p\hat{\theta}_{p} than for both baselines simultaneously.

The thresholds and the sweet-spot condition are characterized explicitly in terms of Φ⁡(λ,m,n)\Phi(\lambda,m,n) in Theorem 7 (Appendix A.6), where the full statement, constants, and proof appear.

Remark 2.

Theorem 2 compares upper bounds on expected regret, not the regrets themselves. However, the thresholds indicate a transition region in validation size: small mm favors training-data methods (unweighted ERM), large mm favors validation-only ERM, and RCIF reduces the bias enough to compete with both in the intermediate regime as observed in Section 7.

7 Experimental results

We evaluate our reweighting scheme across several settings, measuring out-of-sample regret on a clean test set when the training data is corrupted but a small clean validation set is available. To simulate label corruption, we uniformly sample a fraction β\beta (default 0.30.3) of the training points and add isotropic Gaussian noise to their cost labels; the validation and test sets remain clean.

Methods.

We compare ten methods. Iterative Exp. Directed (ours): iterative exponential reweighting with directed score ΨD\Psi^{\text{D}}. Exp. Two-Sided (ours): single-round exponential reweighting with ΨTS\Psi^{\text{TS}}. Directed (ours): additive reweighting pi=1/n+ϕ​ΨiDp_{i}=1/n+\phi\,\Psi^{\text{D}}_{i} with ϕ=0.05\phi=0.05. Unweighted: ERM on the corrupted training set. RC Weight: single-round exponential reweighting using the raw reduced-cost margin ΨjRC=mink∈N⁡(Bj)⁡sk​(c^j,Bj)\Psi^{\text{RC}}_{j}=\min_{k\in N(B_{j})}s_{k}(\hat{c}_{j},B_{j}) as score. Validation Only: ERM on the clean validation set alone. SPO Influence Weight: reweighting via influence functions on the SPO+ surrogate loss rather than reduced costs; the closest analog to our method, isolating the contribution of reduced costs over a surrogate loss (Appendix B.7.4). SPO+ Validation Only: an end-to-end predictor trained by subgradient descent on the SPO+ loss on the validation set alone, initialized at the validation-only least-squares fit. SPO+ Finetune: unweighted ERM on the noisy train-plus-validation pool, fine-tuned by SPO+ subgradient descent on the validation set. Clean ERM (oracle): ERM on the full uncorrupted dataset, a reference lower bound on achievable regret. For all methods except the validation-only ones, we fold the clean validation set into the second-stage fit, assigning each validation point the maximum weight given to any training point, so every method using training data sees the same total data. Additional experiments and details appear in Appendix B.

7.1 Random linear program

We sample a random constraint matrix AA and right-hand side bb defining the downstream LP, and a random linear map θ∗\theta^{*} from features to costs. Training, validation, and test inputs are drawn i.i.d., with cost labels c=θ∗​z+εc=\theta^{*}z+\varepsilon. The upstream predictor is a linear model fit by squared loss. Table 1 reports results with upstream dimension 2020, LP dimension 1010, 2020 constraints, 200200 training points, 5050 validation points, 150150 test points, and corruption rate β=0.3\beta=0.3. Iterative Exp. Directed achieves the lowest regret, the gap to unweighted is modest in this setting but significant under a two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test over seeds (pp = 0.007).

7.2 Shortest path setting

For a more structured downstream LP, we consider the shortest-path problem on a grid network, following Elmachtoub and Grigas (2022): traverse from the northwest to the southeast corner of the grid. We use the PyEPO library (Tang and Khalil, 2022) to generate the dataset with an upstream linear model fit via squared loss. Table 1 reports results on a 4×44\times 4 grid with upstream input dimension 3030, 400400 training points, 100100 validation points, 200200 test points, and β=0.2\beta=0.2. On this more structured problem, RCIF reweighting yields substantially larger gains: Iterative Exp. Directed again performs best, by a much wider margin than in the random LP setting (paired pp <0.048<0.048 for all methods). Furthermore, though the raw magnitude difference between methods is small, the recovery relative to Clean ERM is large: our method recovers 39% of the error induced by noise (0.152 between Clean ERM and Unweighted) whereas the next best method SPO Influence Weight only recovers 30%.

7.3 Neural network upstream

To demonstrate that the method retains value when the upstream predictor is nonlinear, we replace the linear model with a two-layer fully-connected network with hidden dimension 88 and Tanh activation as seen in the last column of Table 1. We use the shortest path setting again, with a 5×45\times 4 grid, upstream input dimension 3030, 200200 training points, 100100 validation points, 200200 test points, and β=0.3\beta=0.3. We compare methods that leave the training procedure unchanged (reweighting and the clean-label reference); the SPO+ Finetune and SPO+ Validation Only baselines are defined for the linear upstream and require a specialized pipeline, so we omit them. Here the additive Directed variant performs best. We conjecture that nonlinearity makes the iterations of Iterative Exp. Directed harmful, since influence-function approximation error compounds across iterations, consistent with the known fragility of influence functions in nonlinear settings (Basu et al., 2020). Correspondingly, the non-iterative Exp. Two-Sided performs relatively better here than in the linear settings, and the Directed variant yields strong improvements through more targeted scoring without added error.

7.4 Validation size study

Now we connect back to our theoretical result in Theorem 2, which provides conditions on the validation set size for which our method has an improved regret upper bound by providing a study on validation set size on shortest path problems (4×\times4 grid, upstream input dimension 20, 500 training points, 200 test points, corruption rate β=0.3\beta=0.3, 100 seeds with validation set varied over {5,10,20,50,100,150}\{5,10,20,50,100,150\}) and observing that it translates to real regret improvements. As the size of the validation set increases, at first, the unweighted method θ^\hat{\theta} outperforms our method, but then for sufficient validation data, our method θ^p\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{p}} wins, but then finally at large validation, θ^val\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{val}} wins. We can visually see this sweet spot where our method wins in Figure 1 on moderate validation set sizes, demonstrating its value in these regimes. See Appendix B.2 for details.

7.5 Misspecification

Similarly to the neural network setting, we test what happens when the upstream model is misspecified. We keep the shortest-path setting (4×44\times 4 grid, input dimension 3030, 400/100/200400/100/200 train/validation/test points, β=0.2\beta=0.2, 5050 seeds) and raise the polynomial degree of PyEPO’s feature-to-cost map from 11 to 22 and 44, so that the true costs are increasingly nonlinear in the features while the predictor remains linear and is fit by squared loss. We report results in Table 2. Raw regret values are not comparable across degrees, since PyEPO rescales the costs with the degree, so each column should be read on its own (degree 1 coincides with Table 1). The gains of RCIF reweighting are preserved and, relative to the corruption damage, grow proportionally with degree: Iterative Exp. Directed attains a test regret of 0.4856±0.01350.4856\pm 0.0135 at degree 22 and 0.2899±0.01150.2899\pm 0.0115 at degree 44, against 0.5715±0.01450.5715\pm 0.0145 and 0.3483±0.01350.3483\pm 0.0135 for unweighted ERM, and it has lower regret than every other competing method. RCIF scores only require the LP geometry at the predicted cost and the first-order response of the predictor, neither of which directly depends on the model being correctly specified, so the mechanism continues to identify harmful training points when the linear fit is only an approximation.

8 Conclusion

We introduced reduced cost influence functions, a downstream-aware signal that propagates training-point influence through the upstream predictor onto the reduced costs of the LP. Building on a score decomposition that isolates clean from corruption-induced contributions, we showed that RCIF scoring decreases the score of directionally corrupted points with high probability, and that there exist validation-size regimes in which RCIF reweighting admits tighter expected-regret upper bounds than unweighted and validation-only ERM. Experiments on random LPs, shortest-path routing, and a neural-network upstream are consistent with these regimes empirically and show consistent gains, particularly for shortest path. The neural-network setting also reveals a limitation: iterating exponential reweighting compounds the approximation error when the upstream is nonlinear, but the non-iterative variant still maintains strong performance. Furthermore, the downstream problem is currently limited to LPs, with assumed nondegeneracy for theoretical results. Promising directions include relaxing the nondegeneracy and connecting with the distance to degeneracy concept, extending the framework to MILPs and convex programs, and combining RCIF scoring with robust regression and active learning techniques for data selection.

A.1 Proof of Lemma 1

RCIF score factorization

Proof.

By definition of the influence function for linear models, the Hessian of the average training loss, viewed as an operator on ℝd×q\mathbb{R}^{d\times q} (vectorized in row-major order), is

Hθ^=1n​∑i=1n∇θ2‖θ​zi−c~i‖2=2​Id⊗Σ^,H_{\hat{\theta}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\nabla_{\theta}^{2}\|\theta z_{i}-\tilde{c}_{i}\|^{2}=2\,I_{d}\otimes\hat{\Sigma},

since the (l1,m1,l2,m2)(l_{1},m_{1};\,l_{2},m_{2}) entry of the Hessian is 2 1[l1=l2](zi)m1(zi)m22\,\mathbf{1}[l_{1}=l_{2}]\,(z_{i})_{m_{1}}(z_{i})_{m_{2}}, and summing gives 2 1[l1=l2]Σ^m1​m22\,\mathbf{1}[l_{1}=l_{2}]\,\hat{\Sigma}_{m_{1}m_{2}}. The inverse is Hθ^−1=12​Id⊗Σ^−1H_{\hat{\theta}}^{-1}=\tfrac{1}{2}\,I_{d}\otimes\hat{\Sigma}^{-1}. Let vec\operatorname{vec} denote row-major vectorization so vec⁡(rj​zj⊤)=rj⊗zj\operatorname{vec}(r_{j}z_{j}^{\top})=r_{j}\otimes z_{j}. The influence function is

vec⁡(Iθ^​(wj))\displaystyle\operatorname{vec}\bigl(I_{\hat{\theta}}(w_{j})\bigr) =−Hθ^−1​vec⁡(∇θℓ)\displaystyle=-H_{\hat{\theta}}^{-1}\operatorname{vec}\bigl(\nabla_{\theta}\ell\bigr)
=−12(Id⊗Σ^−1)⋅2[rj⊗zj]\displaystyle=-\tfrac{1}{2}(I_{d}\otimes\hat{\Sigma}^{-1})\cdot 2\bigl[r_{j}\otimes z_{j}\bigr]
=−(Idrj)⊗(Σ^−1zj)\displaystyle=-(I_{d}\,r_{j})\otimes(\hat{\Sigma}^{-1}z_{j})
=−rj⊗(Σ^−1zj),\displaystyle=-r_{j}\otimes(\hat{\Sigma}^{-1}z_{j}),

where we used the Kronecker product rule (A⊗B)​(u⊗v)=A​u⊗B​v(A\otimes B)(u\otimes v)=Au\otimes Bv. Reshaping back to ℝd×q\mathbb{R}^{d\times q} gives

Iθ^​(wj)=−rj​(Σ^−1​zj)⊤.I_{\hat{\theta}}(w_{j})=-r_{j}\,(\hat{\Sigma}^{-1}z_{j})^{\top}.

Thus by definition of the RCIF, we have

RCIFk,θ^​(zv,wj)\displaystyle\mathrm{RCIF}_{k,\hat{\theta}}(z_{v},w_{j}) =δ​(Bv,k)⊤​∇θfθ^​(zv)​ℐθ^​(wj)\displaystyle=\delta(B_{v},k)^{\top}\,\nabla_{\theta}f_{\hat{\theta}}(z_{v})\,\mathcal{I}_{\hat{\theta}}(w_{j})
=δ​(Bv,k)⊤​ℐθ^​(wj)​zv\displaystyle=\delta(B_{v},k)^{\top}\,\,\mathcal{I}_{\hat{\theta}}(w_{j})z_{v}
=−δ​(Bv,k)⊤​rj​(Σ^−1​zj)⊤​zv\displaystyle=-\delta(B_{v},k)^{\top}\,r_{j}\,(\hat{\Sigma}^{-1}z_{j})^{\top}z_{v}
=−δ​(Bv,k)⊤​rj​κ​(zv,zj)\displaystyle=-\delta(B_{v},k)^{\top}\,r_{j}\kappa(z_{v},z_{j})

where the second equality follows by the directional derivative of a linear function, and the third equality follows by plugging in the derived influence function. ∎

A.2 Proof of Lemma 2

RCIF score decomposition

Proof.

A.3 Score difference in magnitude for corrupted points

Instead of the directed corruption paradigm in Assumption D4, we use the following:

For j∈𝒞j\in\mathcal{C}, c~j=cj+ηj\tilde{c}_{j}=c_{j}+\eta_{j} where ηj\eta_{j} is an additional bounded perturbation such that ηj\eta_{j} is zero-mean and independent from 𝒮,𝒱\mathcal{S},\mathcal{V} and across indices.

We show that the RCIF score magnitude for a fresh sample (independent of 𝒮,𝒱\mathcal{S},\mathcal{V}) that has been corrupted (zj,c~j)=(zj,cj+ηj)(z_{j},\tilde{c}_{j})=(z_{j},c_{j}+\eta_{j}) is larger than the magnitude for uncorrupted version on (zj,cj)(z_{j},c_{j}).

Theorem 3 (Magnitude separation in expectation).

Let (zj,cj)(z_{j},c_{j}) be a fresh sample with cj=θ∗​zj+εjc_{j}=\theta^{*}z_{j}+\varepsilon_{j}, independent of 𝒮\mathcal{S} used to fit θ^\hat{\theta}. Assume the corruption ηj\eta_{j} satisfies

𝔼⁡[ηj∣𝒢]=0,Cov​(ηj∣𝒢)⪰ση2​I,\mathbb{E}[\eta_{j}\mid\mathcal{G}]=0,\qquad\text{Cov}(\eta_{j}\mid\mathcal{G})\succeq\sigma_{\eta}^{2}\,I,

where σ\sigma-algebra 𝒢=σ⁡(θ^,𝒱,zj,cj)\mathcal{G}=\sigma(\hat{\theta},\mathcal{V},z_{j},c_{j}). Let Ψjclean\Psi^{\mathrm{clean}}_{j} be the score evaluated at the clean label (zj,cj)(z_{j},c_{j}) and let Ψj\Psi_{j} be the score evaluated at (zj,c~j)=(zj,cj+ηj)(z_{j},\tilde{c}_{j})=(z_{j},c_{j}+\eta_{j}). Then

𝔼⁡[Ψj2−(Ψjclean)2]≥ση2​𝔼​‖uj‖2≥ 0.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\Psi_{j}^{2}-(\Psi_{j}^{\mathrm{clean}})^{2}\right]\;\geq\;\sigma_{\eta}^{2}\,\mathbb{E}\|u_{j}\|^{2}\;\geq\;0.

where under most distributions the last inequality is strict positivity.

Proof.

By the score decomposition (Lemma 2), Ψj=Ψjclean+uj⊤​ηj\Psi_{j}=\Psi_{j}^{\mathrm{clean}}+u_{j}^{\top}\eta_{j}. Let Δj=uj⊤​ηj\Delta_{j}=u_{j}^{\top}\eta_{j}, so

Ψj2−(Ψjclean)2= 2​Ψjclean​Δj+Δj2.\Psi_{j}^{2}-(\Psi_{j}^{\mathrm{clean}})^{2}\;=\;2\,\Psi_{j}^{\mathrm{clean}}\,\Delta_{j}+\Delta_{j}^{2}.

Since Ψjclean\Psi_{j}^{\mathrm{clean}} and uju_{j} are 𝒢\mathcal{G}-measurable and 𝔼⁡[ηj∣𝒢]=0\mathbb{E}[\eta_{j}\mid\mathcal{G}]=0,

𝔼⁡[Ψjclean​Δj∣𝒢]=Ψjclean​uj⊤​𝔼​[ηj∣𝒢]= 0,\mathbb{E}[\Psi_{j}^{\mathrm{clean}}\,\Delta_{j}\mid\mathcal{G}]\;=\;\Psi_{j}^{\mathrm{clean}}\,u_{j}^{\top}\mathbb{E}[\eta_{j}\mid\mathcal{G}]\;=\;0,

and by the covariance hypothesis,

𝔼⁡[Δj2∣𝒢]=uj⊤​Cov​(ηj∣𝒢)​uj≥ση2​‖uj‖2.\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{j}^{2}\mid\mathcal{G}]\;=\;u_{j}^{\top}\text{Cov}(\eta_{j}\mid\mathcal{G})\,u_{j}\;\geq\;\sigma_{\eta}^{2}\,\|u_{j}\|^{2}.

Taking outer expectation and applying the tower rule gives 𝔼⁡[Ψj2−(Ψjclean)2]≥ση2​𝔼​‖uj‖2≥0\mathbb{E}[\Psi_{j}^{2}-(\Psi_{j}^{\mathrm{clean}})^{2}]\geq\sigma_{\eta}^{2}\,\mathbb{E}\|u_{j}\|^{2}\geq 0. However, we note that 𝔼​‖uj‖2=0\mathbb{E}\|u_{j}\|^{2}=0 only if it is a.s. 0, which is a measure-0 event under reasonable data distributions. ∎

A.4 Statement and proof of Theorem 1

Theorem 4 (Decreased corruption score under alignment).

Adopt Assumptions (D1)–(D5). Let (zj,cj)(z_{j},c_{j}) be a fresh sample drawn from 𝒟\mathcal{D} independently of θ^\hat{\theta} (fit on 𝒮\mathcal{S}) and of 𝒱\mathcal{V}, and let c~j=cj+ηj\tilde{c}_{j}=c_{j}+\eta_{j} be its directional corruption (D4). P⁡(Ψj−Ψjclean≥−α⁡(γ−t)|ℱ)≤exp⁡(−m​t22​Mγ2),P\!\left(\Psi_{j}-\Psi_{j}^{\mathrm{clean}}\;\geq\;-\alpha(\gamma-t)\,\middle|\,\mathcal{F}\right)\;\leq\;\exp\!\left(-\frac{m\,t^{2}}{2M_{\gamma}^{2}}\right),

A.5 In-sample signed decreased corruption scoring

Theorem 4 assumes that the corrupted point (zj,c~j)=(zj,cj+ηj)(z_{j},\tilde{c}_{j})=(z_{j},c_{j}+\eta_{j}) (where ηj\eta_{j} is a bounded directional corruption as in Assumption D4) is independent of the fitted estimator θ^\hat{\theta}. However, we would like to see that if wjw_{j} is one of the training points used to fit θ^\hat{\theta}, that Theorem 4 still holds. We show that under additional mild regularity assumptions, the conclusion of Theorem 4 continues to hold for in-sample jj, with an additive O⁡(1/n)O(1/n) slack.

We replace θ^\hat{\theta} everywhere in the score by the leave-one-out estimator θ^−j\hat{\theta}_{-j}, which is independent of wjw_{j} by construction, and control the resulting approximation error.

Notation.

Let

θ^−j:=arg​minθ⁡1n−1​∑i≠j‖θ​zi−c~i‖2,Σ^−j:=1n−1​∑i≠jzi​zi⊤,\hat{\theta}_{-j}\;:=\;\argmin_{\theta}\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i\neq j}\|\theta z_{i}-\tilde{c}_{i}\|^{2},\qquad\hat{\Sigma}_{-j}\;:=\;\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i\neq j}z_{i}z_{i}^{\top},

κ−(z,z′):=z⊤Σ^−j−1z′,Ψjloo:=−1m∑v∈𝒱σv−δ(Bv−,kv∗⁣−)⊤rj−κ−(zv,zj),\kappa^{-}(z,z^{\prime})\;:=\;z^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}_{-j}^{-1}z^{\prime},\qquad\Psi_{j}^{\mathrm{loo}}\;:=\;-\frac{1}{m}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\sigma_{v}^{-}\,\delta(B_{v}^{-},k_{v}^{*-})^{\top}r_{j}^{-}\,\kappa^{-}(z_{v},z_{j}),

Thus Ψjloo\Psi_{j}^{\mathrm{loo}} is the score one would compute by substituting θ^−j\hat{\theta}_{-j} for θ^\hat{\theta} throughout the score formula.

Assumption 3.

Note that by D1, the leverage satisfies hj≤R2/(n​μ)h_{j}\leq R^{2}/(n\mu), so hj→0h_{j}\to 0 at rate 1/n1/n and 1−hj≥1/21-h_{j}\geq 1/2 for n≥2​R2/μn\geq 2R^{2}/\mu.

Lemma 3 (Exact LOO identities for linear ERM).

Suppose hj<1h_{j}<1. Then

θ^−j−θ^\displaystyle\hat{\theta}_{-j}-\hat{\theta} =1n⁡(1−hj)​rj​(Σ^−1​zj)⊤,\displaystyle\;=\;\frac{1}{n(1-h_{j})}\,r_{j}\,(\hat{\Sigma}^{-1}z_{j})^{\top}, (1)

We now make an assumption that the optimal bases of predictions by θ^\hat{\theta} and θ^−j\hat{\theta}_{-j} are similar.

Assumption 4 (Validation basis stability under LOO).

For every v∈𝒱v\in\mathcal{V}, the optimal basis BvB_{v}, the fragile direction kv∗k_{v}^{*}, and the correctness sign σv\sigma_{v} are unchanged when c^v\hat{c}_{v} is replaced by c^v−\hat{c}_{v}^{-}, i.e. Bv−=BvB_{v}^{-}=B_{v}, kv∗⁣−=kv∗k_{v}^{*-}=k_{v}^{*}, and σv−=σv\sigma_{v}^{-}=\sigma_{v}.

This is a reasonable assumption which we briefly justify: it holds as nn increases.

Remark 3 (One sufficient condition for Assumption 4 with two-sided scoring).

Given (D1)-(D5), and that for every v∈𝒱v\in\mathcal{V} the second-smallest normalized reduced cost at c^v\hat{c}_{v} (by normalized reduced cost we mean sk​(c^v,Bv)‖δ⁡(Bv,k)‖\frac{s_{k}(\hat{c}_{v},B_{v})}{\left\lVert\delta(B_{v},k)\right\rVert}) exceeds the smallest by at least 2​ρ2\rho, with the smallest value at least ≥ρ\geq\rho, where

ρ>R2​Rrn​μ​(1−hj).\rho\;>\;\frac{R^{2}R_{r}}{n\mu(1-h_{j})}.

Then Assumption 4 holds, assuming two-sided score.

Proof.

By Lemma 3, ‖θ^−j−θ^‖op≤‖rj‖​‖Σ^−1​zj‖n⁡(1−hj)≤R​Rrn​μ​(1−hj)\|\hat{\theta}_{-j}-\hat{\theta}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\frac{\|r_{j}\|\,\|\hat{\Sigma}^{-1}z_{j}\|}{n(1-h_{j})}\leq\frac{RR_{r}}{n\mu(1-h_{j})}, so ‖c^v−c^v−‖≤R2​Rr/(n​μ​(1−hj))\|\hat{c}_{v}-\hat{c}_{v}^{-}\|\leq R^{2}R_{r}/(n\mu(1-h_{j})). For any unit direction δ⁡(B,k)/‖δ⁡(B,k)‖\delta(B,k)/\|\delta(B,k)\|, by Cauchy-Schwarz

|sk​(c^v−,B)/‖δ⁡(B,k)‖−sk​(c^v,B)/‖δ⁡(B,k)‖|≤‖c^v−c^v−‖.\bigl|s_{k}(\hat{c}_{v}^{-},B)/\|\delta(B,k)\|-s_{k}(\hat{c}_{v},B)/\|\delta(B,k)\|\bigr|\;\leq\;\|\hat{c}_{v}-\hat{c}_{v}^{-}\|.

Hence each normalized reduced cost shifts by less than ρ\rho. Since the smallest is at least ρ\rho and the gap to the second-smallest exceeds 2​ρ2\rho, signs of all reduced costs are preserved (so Bv−=BvB_{v}^{-}=B_{v}) and the argmin is preserved (so kv∗⁣−=kv∗k_{v}^{*-}=k_{v}^{*}). The sign σv\sigma_{v} is also preserved since Bv−=BvB_{v}^{-}=B_{v}. ∎

Assumption 4 is imposed for the chosen scoring rule. Remark 3 gives one sufficient condition for Assumption 4 in the two-sided scoring case.

Lemma 4 (LOO stability of the RCIF score).

Under Assumptions (D1)-(D5) and 4,

|Ψj−Ψjloo|≤Cn​(‖rj‖),|\Psi_{j}-\Psi_{j}^{\mathrm{loo}}|\;\leq\;\frac{C}{n}\,\bigl(\|r_{j}\|\bigr),

uj=1m​∑v∈𝒱σv​κ​(zv,zj)​δ​(Bv,kv∗),u_{j}\;=\;\frac{1}{m}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\sigma_{v}\,\kappa(z_{v},z_{j})\,\delta(B_{v},k_{v}^{*}),

uj−−uj=1m​∑v∈𝒱σv​(κ−​(zv,zj)−κ⁡(zv,zj))​δ​(Bv,kv∗).u_{j}^{-}-u_{j}\;=\;\frac{1}{m}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\sigma_{v}\,(\kappa^{-}(z_{v},z_{j})-\kappa(z_{v},z_{j}))\,\delta(B_{v},k_{v}^{*}).

|Ψj−Ψjloo|\displaystyle|\Psi_{j}-\Psi_{j}^{\mathrm{loo}}| ≤|uj⊤​(rj−rj−)|+|(uj−uj−)⊤​rj−|\displaystyle\;\leq\;|u_{j}^{\top}(r_{j}-r_{j}^{-})|+|(u_{j}-u_{j}^{-})^{\top}r_{j}^{-}|
≤‖uj‖​c2​‖rj‖/n+(c1/n)​‖rj−‖\displaystyle\;\leq\;\|u_{j}\|\,c_{2}\|r_{j}\|/n+(c_{1}/n)\,\|r_{j}^{-}\|

Now we can show the in-sample result.

In-sample setup.

For the in-sample variant, the σ\sigma-algebra of interest is ℱ−:=σ⁡(θ^−j,zj,cj)\mathcal{F}^{-}:=\sigma(\hat{\theta}_{-j},z_{j},c_{j}), under which corruption ηj=−α​δ^j\eta_{j}=-\alpha\hat{\delta}_{j} is independent of θ^−j\hat{\theta}_{-j}. Ψjloo=Ψjloo,clean+(uj−)⊤​ηj,Ψjloo,clean:=−(uj−)⊤​rj−,clean,\Psi_{j}^{\mathrm{loo}}\;=\;\Psi_{j}^{\text{loo,clean}}+(u_{j}^{-})^{\top}\eta_{j},\qquad\Psi_{j}^{\text{loo,clean}}\;:=\;-(u_{j}^{-})^{\top}r_{j}^{-,\text{clean}},

where rj−,clean:=θ^−j​zj−cjr_{j}^{-,\text{clean}}:=\hat{\theta}_{-j}z_{j}-c_{j}.

Theorem 5 (Signed score decrease, in-sample variant).

Adopt Assumptions (D1)-(D5) and Assumptions 3, 4. Let γ−:=γ⁡(θ^−j,zj,cj)>0\gamma^{-}:=\gamma(\hat{\theta}_{-j},z_{j},c_{j})>0 be the validation alignment evaluated at the LOO estimator, and let C,C′C,C^{\prime} be the coefficients from Lemma 4.     (Expectation)

    (High probability) For every t∈(0,γ−)t\in(0,\gamma^{-}), on the event of probability ≥1−exp(−mt2/(2Mγ2))\geq 1-\exp(-mt^{2}/(2M_{\gamma}^{2})) guaranteed by Theorem 4,

    Δj≤−α⁡(γ−−t)+2​C′+C​αn.\Delta_{j}\;\leq\;-\alpha(\gamma^{-}-t)+\frac{2C^{\prime}+C\alpha}{n}.

    In particular, taking t=γ−/2t=\gamma^{-}/2 and assuming n≥(8​C′+4​C​α)/(α​γ−)n\geq(8C^{\prime}+4C\alpha)/(\alpha\gamma^{-}),

    Δj≤−α​γ−4\Delta_{j}\;\leq\;-\frac{\alpha\gamma^{-}}{4}

    on an event of probability ≥1−exp(−m(γ−)2/(8Mγ2))\geq 1-\exp(-m(\gamma^{-})^{2}/(8M_{\gamma}^{2})).

Proof.

Let Δjloo:=(uj−)⊤​ηj\Delta_{j}^{\mathrm{loo}}:=(u_{j}^{-})^{\top}\eta_{j}. Since θ^−j\hat{\theta}_{-j} is independent of wjw_{j}, the proof of Theorem 4 applies verbatim to Δjloo\Delta_{j}^{\mathrm{loo}}, yielding

𝔼⁡[Δjloo∣ℱ−]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{j}^{\mathrm{loo}}\mid\mathcal{F}^{-}] =−α​γ−,\displaystyle\;=\;-\alpha\gamma^{-},
P⁡(Δjloo≥−α⁡(γ−−t)|ℱ−)\displaystyle P\!\left(\Delta_{j}^{\mathrm{loo}}\geq-\alpha(\gamma^{-}-t)\,\middle|\,\mathcal{F}^{-}\right) ≤exp(−mt2/(2Mγ2)).\displaystyle\;\leq\;\exp(-mt^{2}/(2M_{\gamma}^{2})).

By Lemma 4 applied at both rjr_{j} (full score) and rjcleanr_{j}^{\text{clean}} (clean score) which incurs an extra corruption ηj\eta_{j} term, (via Assumption 3 and ‖ηj‖≤α\|\eta_{j}\|\leq\alpha),

|Δj−Δjloo|=|Ψj−Ψjclean−Ψjloo+Ψjloo, clean|≤2​C′+C​αn.|\Delta_{j}-\Delta_{j}^{\mathrm{loo}}|\;=\;|\Psi_{j}-\Psi_{j}^{\text{clean}}-\Psi_{j}^{\mathrm{loo}}+\Psi_{j}^{\text{loo, clean}}|\;\leq\;\frac{2C^{\prime}+C\alpha}{n}.

Substituting into each statement of Theorem 4 gives parts (1) and (2). ∎

Remark 4.

For nn large enough the in-sample guarantee of Theorem 5 is qualitatively the same as the cross-fit version. The replacement of γ\gamma by γ−\gamma^{-} is harmless for our purposes since γ−→γ\gamma^{-}\to\gamma as n→∞n\to\infty (because θ^−j→θ^\hat{\theta}_{-j}\to\hat{\theta} at rate 1/n1/n, and the alignment parameter is continuous in the estimator under Assumption 4).

A.6 Statement and proof of Theorem 2

In Appendix Subsection A.5 we showed that a single corrupted point receives a lower score with high probability. We now aggregate this across the corruption set to obtain an unconditional expected reduction of the worst-case corrupted bias of the weighted ERM, relative to θ^\hat{\theta} and θ^val\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{val}}. Under constant-rate, constant-magnitude corruption, no estimator using only the corrupted training data can drive corruption bias to zero, but RCIF reweighting reduces the constant.

Then we may translate the reduction in bias to regret (under the simplifying assumption 2).

A.6.1 Bounding weight ratio between clean and corrupted points

Remark 5.

Under (D1)–(D5) and Assumption 3 let M=Rr​D​R2/μM=R_{r}DR^{2}/\mu, and observe that |Ψj|<M,a.s.∀j|\Psi_{j}|<M,\ a.s.\ \forall j.

We work with the leave-one-out objects of Appendix A.5: θ^−j\hat{\theta}_{-j}, κ−​(z,z′):=z⊤​Σ^−j−1​z′\kappa^{-}(z,z^{\prime}):=z^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}_{-j}^{-1}z^{\prime}, and the LOO score aggregator

uj(−1):=1m​∑v∈𝒱σv−​κ−​(zj,zv)​δ​(Bv−,kv∗⁣−).u_{j}^{(-1)}\;:=\;\frac{1}{m}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\sigma_{v}^{-}\,\kappa^{-}(z_{j},z_{v})\,\delta(B_{v}^{-},k_{v}^{*-}).

Quantities of interest

For linear/squared-loss ERM, the parameter error decomposes as

θ^p−θ⋆=(∑i=1npi​εi​zi⊤+Tw)​Σ^W−1,Σ^W:=∑ipi​zi​zi⊤,\hat{\theta}_{p}-\theta^{\star}\;=\;\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\,\varepsilon_{i}z_{i}^{\top}\;+\;T_{w}\Bigr)\,\hat{\Sigma}_{W}^{-1},\qquad\hat{\Sigma}_{W}:=\sum_{i}p_{i}z_{i}z_{i}^{\top},

and analogously for the unweighted ERM with pi=1/np_{i}=1/n. Define the corruption-bias matrices

T0:=1n​∑j∈𝒞(−α​δ^j)​zj⊤,Tw:=∑j∈𝒞pj​(−α​δ^j)​zj⊤,T_{0}:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{C}}(-\alpha\,\hat{\delta}_{j})z_{j}^{\top},\qquad T_{w}:=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{C}}p_{j}(-\alpha\,\hat{\delta}_{j})z_{j}^{\top},

which directly drive the corruption bias of the corresponding estimators.

We note that we can reduce the problem from the corruption set to one corrupt index, due to Assumptions D1 and D3.

Lemma 5 (Exchangeability of corruption).

For any sequence (Fj)(F_{j}) such that the joint law of (Fj,𝟏j∈𝒞)j=1n(F_{j},\mathbf{1}_{j\in\mathcal{C}})_{j=1}^{n} is permutation-invariant,

𝔼⁡[∑j∈𝒞Fj]=n​β​𝔼​[F1∣1∈𝒞].\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{j\in\mathcal{C}}F_{j}\right]\;=\;n\beta\,\mathbb{E}[F_{1}\mid 1\in\mathcal{C}].
Proof.

By (D3), (𝟏1∈𝒞,…,𝟏n∈𝒞)(\mathbf{1}_{1\in\mathcal{C}},\ldots,\mathbf{1}_{n\in\mathcal{C}}) is exchangeable with marginal mean β\beta. By (D1)–(D2), (zi,εi)(z_{i},\varepsilon_{i}) are iid, so the joint law of (wi,𝟏i∈𝒞)i=1n(w_{i},\mathbf{1}_{i\in\mathcal{C}})_{i=1}^{n} is permutation-invariant. Hence 𝔼⁡[𝟏j∈𝒞​Fj]=𝔼⁡[𝟏1∈𝒞​F1]\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_{j\in\mathcal{C}}F_{j}]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_{1\in\mathcal{C}}F_{1}] for every jj, and summing nn identical terms with Pr⁡(1∈𝒞)=β\Pr(1\in\mathcal{C})=\beta gives the claim. ∎

Remark 6 (Deterministic bound on the score sum).

Under (D1)–(D5) and Assumption 3, since |Ψi|≤M|\Psi_{i}|\leq M a.s., the sum of scores

Q:=∑i=1neλ​ΨiQ:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}e^{\lambda\Psi_{i}}

admits the deterministic lower bound Q≥n​e−λ​MQ\geq n\,e^{-\lambda M} a.s., and hence 1/Q≤eλ​M/n1/Q\leq e^{\lambda M}/n a.s.

Lemma 6 (Weight-ratio contraction for a clean vs corrupted point).

Focusing on the first training index, and under Assumption 4, let

Φ𝒞​(λ):=𝔼⁡[eλ​Ψ1∣1∈𝒞],Φ𝒞¯​(λ):=𝔼⁡[eλ​Ψ1∣1∉𝒞].\Phi_{\mathcal{C}}(\lambda):=\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda\Psi_{1}}\mid 1\in\mathcal{C}],\qquad\Phi_{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}(\lambda):=\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda\Psi_{1}}\mid 1\notin\mathcal{C}].

Under (D1)–(D5), Assumptions 1 and 3, for every λ>0\lambda>0,

Φ𝒞​(λ)Φ𝒞¯​(λ)≤e−λαγ0/4+e2​λ​M(δγ+e−mγ02/(8Mγ2))+O(1/n).\frac{\Phi_{\mathcal{C}}(\lambda)}{\Phi_{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}(\lambda)}\;\leq\;e^{-\lambda\alpha\gamma_{0}/4}\;+\;e^{2\lambda M}\bigl(\delta_{\gamma}+e^{-m\gamma_{0}^{2}/(8M_{\gamma}^{2})}\bigr)\;+\;O(1/n).

We define the contraction factor

Φ(λ,m,n):=e−λαγ0/4+e2​λ​M(δγ+e−mγ02/(8Mγ2))+O(1/n).\Phi(\lambda,m,n)\;:=\;e^{-\lambda\alpha\gamma_{0}/4}\;+\;e^{2\lambda M}\bigl(\delta_{\gamma}+e^{-m\gamma_{0}^{2}/(8M_{\gamma}^{2})}\bigr)\;+\;O(1/n).
Proof.

Recall the score decomposition (Lemma 2) applied at θ^−1\hat{\theta}_{-1}:

Ψ1=Ψ1loo+O⁡(1/n)=Ψ1cf−α​u1(−1)⊤​δ^1⋅𝟏1∈𝒞+O⁡(1/n),\Psi_{1}\;=\;\Psi_{1}^{\mathrm{loo}}+O(1/n)\;=\;\Psi_{1}^{\mathrm{cf}}-\alpha\,u_{1}^{(-1)\top}\hat{\delta}_{1}\cdot\mathbf{1}_{1\in\mathcal{C}}+O(1/n),

where Ψ1cf:=−u1(−1)⊤​(θ^−1​z1−c1)\Psi_{1}^{\mathrm{cf}}:=-u_{1}^{(-1)\top}(\hat{\theta}_{-1}z_{1}-c_{1}) (which represents the counterfactual score) depends only on θ^−1,𝒱,z1,c1\hat{\theta}_{-1},\mathcal{V},z_{1},c_{1}, using the clean cost c1c_{1}.

Step 1: pointwise bound on the corruption shift. Define the high-probability event

ℱ:={γ(θ^−1,z1,c1)≥γ0}∩{u1(−1)⊤δ^1≥γ0/2}.\mathcal{F}\;:=\;\bigl\{\gamma(\hat{\theta}_{-1},z_{1},c_{1})\geq\gamma_{0}\bigr\}\cap\bigl\{u_{1}^{(-1)\top}\hat{\delta}_{1}\geq\gamma_{0}/2\bigr\}.

By Assumption 1, Pr[γ(θ^−1,z1,c1)<γ0]≤δγ\Pr[\gamma(\hat{\theta}_{-1},z_{1},c_{1})<\gamma_{0}]\leq\delta_{\gamma}. Conditional on γ⁡(θ^−1,z1,c1)≥γ0\gamma(\hat{\theta}_{-1},z_{1},c_{1})\geq\gamma_{0}, Hoeffding’s inequality applied to the iid bounded summands WvW_{v} defining u1(−1)⊤​δ^1=1m​∑vWvu_{1}^{(-1)\top}\hat{\delta}_{1}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{v}W_{v} (cf. Theorem 5) gives

Pr[u1(−1)⊤δ^1<γ0/2∣γ≥γ0]≤e−mγ02/(8Mγ2).\Pr[u_{1}^{(-1)\top}\hat{\delta}_{1}<\gamma_{0}/2\mid\gamma\geq\gamma_{0}]\;\leq\;e^{-m\gamma_{0}^{2}/(8M_{\gamma}^{2})}.

By a union bound, Pr[ℱc]≤δγ+e−mγ02/(8Mγ2)\Pr[\mathcal{F}^{c}]\leq\delta_{\gamma}+e^{-m\gamma_{0}^{2}/(8M_{\gamma}^{2})}.

Step 2: bound on Φ𝒞\Phi_{\mathcal{C}}. Conditional on {1∈𝒞}\{1\in\mathcal{C}\}, decompose

𝔼⁡[eλ​Ψ1]=𝔼⁡[eλ​Ψ1​ 1ℱ]+𝔼⁡[eλ​Ψ1​ 1ℱc].\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{\lambda\Psi_{1}}\bigr]\;=\;\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{\lambda\Psi_{1}}\,\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{F}}\bigr]\;+\;\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{\lambda\Psi_{1}}\,\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{F}^{c}}\bigr].

On ℱ\mathcal{F}, Ψ1≤Ψ1cf−α​γ0/2+O⁡(1/n)\Psi_{1}\leq\Psi_{1}^{\mathrm{cf}}-\alpha\gamma_{0}/2+O(1/n), so

𝔼[eλ​Ψ1 1ℱ∣1∈𝒞]≤e−λαγ0/2+O(λ/n)𝔼[eλ​Ψ1cf∣1∈𝒞].\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{\lambda\Psi_{1}}\,\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{F}}\mid 1\in\mathcal{C}\bigr]\;\leq\;e^{-\lambda\alpha\gamma_{0}/2+O(\lambda/n)}\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{\lambda\Psi_{1}^{\mathrm{cf}}}\mid 1\in\mathcal{C}\bigr].

Off ℱ\mathcal{F}, |Ψ1|≤M|\Psi_{1}|\leq M gives

𝔼[eλ​Ψ1 1ℱc∣1∈𝒞]≤eλ​M(δγ+e−mγ02/(8Mγ2)).\mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{\lambda\Psi_{1}}\,\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{F}^{c}}\mid 1\in\mathcal{C}\bigr]\;\leq\;e^{\lambda M}\bigl(\delta_{\gamma}+e^{-m\gamma_{0}^{2}/(8M_{\gamma}^{2})}\bigr).

Step 3: counterfactual-MGF identification. We show that

𝔼⁡[eλ​Ψ1cf∣1∈𝒞]=Φ𝒞¯​(λ)+O⁡(1/n).\mathbb{E}\!\left[e^{\lambda\Psi_{1}^{\mathrm{cf}}}\mid 1\in\mathcal{C}\right]\;=\;\Phi_{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}(\lambda)\;+\;O(1/n). (4)

The counterfactual score Ψ1cf\Psi_{1}^{\mathrm{cf}} depends on the clean data (z1,c1)(z_{1},c_{1}) and the LOO estimator θ^−1\hat{\theta}_{-1}. Its conditional distribution given {1∈𝒞}\{1\in\mathcal{C}\} differs from its distribution given {1∉𝒞}\{1\notin\mathcal{C}\} only through θ^−1\hat{\theta}_{-1}: in the first case θ^−1\hat{\theta}_{-1} is fit on a sample with |𝒞|−1|\mathcal{C}|-1 corrupted points among {2,…,n}\{2,\ldots,n\}, in the second on a sample with |𝒞||\mathcal{C}| corrupted points. The marginal of (z1,c1)(z_{1},c_{1}) is identical in both cases since corruption assignment is independent of the clean data.

Coupling. We bound the difference between the two conditional expectations via a coupling. Sample uniformly from the clean data (zi,ci)i=2n(z_{i},c_{i})_{i=2}^{n}, a subset SS of size |𝒞|−1|\mathcal{C}|-1, and an additional index j⋆∈{2,…,n}∖Sj^{\star}\in\{2,\ldots,n\}\setminus S. Define two parallel LOO estimators on the same probability space:

  • •

    θ^−1A\hat{\theta}_{-1}^{A}, fit with corruption set CSC_{S} inside {2,…,n}\{2,\ldots,n\} (corresponding to 1∈𝒞1\in\mathcal{C}).

  • •

    θ^−1B\hat{\theta}_{-1}^{B}, fit with corruption set CS∪{j⋆}C_{S}\cup\{j^{\star}\} inside {2,…,n}\{2,\ldots,n\} (corresponding to 1∉𝒞1\notin\mathcal{C}).

By construction, the marginals of θ^−1A\hat{\theta}_{-1}^{A} and θ^−1B\hat{\theta}_{-1}^{B} coincide with the conditional distributions of θ^−1\hat{\theta}_{-1} given {1∈𝒞}\{1\in\mathcal{C}\} and {1∉𝒞}\{1\notin\mathcal{C}\} respectively, and θ^−1A\hat{\theta}_{-1}^{A}, θ^−1B\hat{\theta}_{-1}^{B} differ only in the corruption status of one training index, j⋆j^{\star}. Lemma 3 then gives

‖θ^−1A−θ^−1B‖=O⁡(1/n)a.s.,\bigl\|\hat{\theta}_{-1}^{A}-\hat{\theta}_{-1}^{B}\bigr\|\;=\;O(1/n)\quad\text{a.s.,}

and by Lemma 4 yields

|Ψ1cf,A−Ψ1cf,B|=O⁡(1/n)a.s.\bigl|\Psi_{1}^{\mathrm{cf},A}-\Psi_{1}^{\mathrm{cf},B}\bigr|\;=\;O(1/n)\quad\text{a.s.}

Bound on the expected corruption difference. On the coupling space, using |ea−eb|≤emax⁡(a,b)​|a−b||e^{a}-e^{b}|\leq e^{\max(a,b)}|a-b| and |Ψ1cf|≤M|\Psi_{1}^{\mathrm{cf}}|\leq M:

|eλ​Ψ1cf,A−eλ​Ψ1cf,B|≤λ​eλ​M​|Ψ1cf,A−Ψ1cf,B|=O⁡(1/n)a.s.\bigl|e^{\lambda\Psi_{1}^{\mathrm{cf},A}}-e^{\lambda\Psi_{1}^{\mathrm{cf},B}}\bigr|\;\leq\;\lambda\,e^{\lambda M}\,\bigl|\Psi_{1}^{\mathrm{cf},A}-\Psi_{1}^{\mathrm{cf},B}\bigr|\;=\;O(1/n)\quad\text{a.s.}

Taking expectations and applying Jensen’s inequality:

|𝔼⁡[eλ​Ψ1cf,A]−𝔼⁡[eλ​Ψ1cf,B]|≤𝔼​|eλ​Ψ1cf,A−eλ​Ψ1cf,B|=O⁡(1/n).\bigl|\,\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda\Psi_{1}^{\mathrm{cf},A}}]-\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda\Psi_{1}^{\mathrm{cf},B}}]\,\bigr|\;\leq\;\mathbb{E}\bigl|e^{\lambda\Psi_{1}^{\mathrm{cf},A}}-e^{\lambda\Psi_{1}^{\mathrm{cf},B}}\bigr|\;=\;O(1/n).

The marginal-matching property of the coupling identifies the two expectations on the left with the conditional expectations of interest:

|𝔼⁡[eλ​Ψ1cf∣1∈𝒞]−𝔼⁡[eλ​Ψ1cf∣1∉𝒞]|=O⁡(1/n).\bigl|\,\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda\Psi_{1}^{\mathrm{cf}}}\mid 1\in\mathcal{C}]-\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda\Psi_{1}^{\mathrm{cf}}}\mid 1\notin\mathcal{C}]\,\bigr|\;=\;O(1/n).

See that on the event {1∉𝒞}\{1\notin\mathcal{C}\} the counterfactual coincides with the actual score, Ψ1cf=Ψ1\Psi_{1}^{\mathrm{cf}}=\Psi_{1}, and therefore 𝔼⁡[eλ​Ψ1cf∣1∉𝒞]=Φ𝒞¯​(λ)\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda\Psi_{1}^{\mathrm{cf}}}\mid 1\notin\mathcal{C}]=\Phi_{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}(\lambda). Substituting yields (4).

Step 4: combine and divide. Substituting (4) into the first conclusion of Step 2 gives

Φ𝒞​(λ)\displaystyle\Phi_{\mathcal{C}}(\lambda) ≤e−λαγ0/2+O(λ/n)[Φ𝒞¯(λ)+O(1/n)]+eλ​M(δγ+e−mγ02/(8Mγ2))\displaystyle\leq e^{-\lambda\alpha\gamma_{0}/2+O(\lambda/n)}\bigl[\Phi_{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}(\lambda)+O(1/n)\bigr]\;+\;e^{\lambda M}\bigl(\delta_{\gamma}+e^{-m\gamma_{0}^{2}/(8M_{\gamma}^{2})}\bigr)
=e−λαγ0/2(1+O(λ/n))Φ𝒞¯(λ)+O(1/n)+eλ​M(δγ+e−mγ02/(8Mγ2)),\displaystyle=e^{-\lambda\alpha\gamma_{0}/2}\,(1+O(\lambda/n))\,\Phi_{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}(\lambda)\;+\;O(1/n)\;+\;e^{\lambda M}\bigl(\delta_{\gamma}+e^{-m\gamma_{0}^{2}/(8M_{\gamma}^{2})}\bigr), (5)

where the second line uses e−λαγ0/2+O(λ/n)=e−λαγ0/2(1+O(λ/n))e^{-\lambda\alpha\gamma_{0}/2+O(\lambda/n)}=e^{-\lambda\alpha\gamma_{0}/2}(1+O(\lambda/n)) via first order Taylor expansion together with the boundedness Φ𝒞¯​(λ)≤eλ​M\Phi_{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}(\lambda)\leq e^{\lambda M} and e−λαγ0/2+O(λ/n)=O(1)e^{-\lambda\alpha\gamma_{0}/2+O(\lambda/n)}=O(1) to absorb the cross-term e−λαγ0/2+O(λ/n)⋅O(1/n)e^{-\lambda\alpha\gamma_{0}/2+O(\lambda/n)}\!\cdot\!O(1/n) into the O⁡(1/n)O(1/n) term.

To divide both sides by Φ𝒞¯​(λ)\Phi_{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}(\lambda), we use the deterministic lower bound

Φ𝒞¯​(λ)=𝔼⁡[eλ​Ψ1∣1∉𝒞]≥e−λ​M,\Phi_{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}(\lambda)\;=\;\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda\Psi_{1}}\mid 1\notin\mathcal{C}]\;\geq\;e^{-\lambda M}, (6)

which follows from Ψ1≥−M\Psi_{1}\geq-M a.s. In particular 1/Φ𝒞¯​(λ)≤eλ​M1/\Phi_{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}(\lambda)\leq e^{\lambda M}.

Dividing (5) term by term and applying (6):

Φ𝒞​(λ)Φ𝒞¯​(λ)\displaystyle\frac{\Phi_{\mathcal{C}}(\lambda)}{\Phi_{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}(\lambda)} ≤e−λαγ0/2(1+O(λ/n))+O⁡(1/n)Φ𝒞¯​(λ)+eλ​M(δγ+e−mγ02/(8Mγ2))Φ𝒞¯​(λ)\displaystyle\leq e^{-\lambda\alpha\gamma_{0}/2}\,(1+O(\lambda/n))\;+\;\frac{O(1/n)}{\Phi_{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}(\lambda)}\;+\;\frac{e^{\lambda M}\bigl(\delta_{\gamma}+e^{-m\gamma_{0}^{2}/(8M_{\gamma}^{2})}\bigr)}{\Phi_{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}(\lambda)}
≤e−λαγ0/2+e2​λ​M(δγ+e−mγ02/(8Mγ2))+O(1/n),\displaystyle\leq e^{-\lambda\alpha\gamma_{0}/2}\;+\;e^{2\lambda M}\bigl(\delta_{\gamma}+e^{-m\gamma_{0}^{2}/(8M_{\gamma}^{2})}\bigr)\;+\;O(1/n),

where we have folded the O⁡(λ/n)O(\lambda/n) slack on the leading term into the additive O⁡(1/n)O(1/n) remainder.

Finally, since e−λαγ0/2≤e−λαγ0/4e^{-\lambda\alpha\gamma_{0}/2}\leq e^{-\lambda\alpha\gamma_{0}/4} for λ,α,γ0>0\lambda,\alpha,\gamma_{0}>0, we may relax the leading exponent for notational consistency with Theorem 5, obtaining

Φ𝒞​(λ)Φ𝒞¯​(λ)≤e−λαγ0/4+e2​λ​M(δγ+e−mγ02/(8Mγ2))+O(1/n),\frac{\Phi_{\mathcal{C}}(\lambda)}{\Phi_{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}(\lambda)}\;\leq\;e^{-\lambda\alpha\gamma_{0}/4}\;+\;e^{2\lambda M}\bigl(\delta_{\gamma}+e^{-m\gamma_{0}^{2}/(8M_{\gamma}^{2})}\bigr)\;+\;O(1/n),

which is the conclusion of the lemma. ∎

A.6.2 Bounding moments of bias corruption term

Theorem 6 (Expected corruption-bias contraction).

Under Assumptions 1,  3, 4, and (D1)–(D5), the expected corruption-bias matrix of the reweighted estimator satisfies

𝔼​‖Tw‖F≤α​β​R​e2​λ​M​Φ​(λ,m,n),\mathbb{E}\|T_{w}\|_{F}\;\leq\;\alpha\beta R\,e^{2\lambda M}\,\Phi(\lambda,m,n), (7)

where Φ⁡(λ,m,n)\Phi(\lambda,m,n) is the weight ratio bound in Lemma 6. The unweighted estimator’s corruption bias satisfies the deterministic bound

𝔼​‖T0‖F≤α​β​R.\mathbb{E}\|T_{0}\|_{F}\;\leq\;\alpha\beta R. (8)

The reweighted bound improves on the unweighted bound by the multiplicative factor e2​λ​M​Φ​(λ,m,n)e^{2\lambda M}\,\Phi(\lambda,m,n), which is strictly less than 11 whenever Φ⁡(λ,m,n)<e−2​λ​M\Phi(\lambda,m,n)<e^{-2\lambda M}.

Second-moment equivalents.

𝔼​‖Tw‖F2≤α2​β​R2​e2​λ​M​Φ​(λ,m,n),\mathbb{E}\|T_{w}\|_{F}^{2}\;\leq\;\alpha^{2}\beta R^{2}\,e^{2\lambda M}\,\Phi(\lambda,m,n), (9)
𝔼​‖T0‖F2≤α2​β2​R2.\mathbb{E}\|T_{0}\|_{F}^{2}\;\leq\;\alpha^{2}\beta^{2}R^{2}. (10)

The reweighted second-moment bound improves on the unweighted one by the multiplicative factor e2​λ​M​Φ​(λ,m,n)/βe^{2\lambda M}\,\Phi(\lambda,m,n)/\beta, which is strictly less than 11 whenever Φ⁡(λ,m,n)<β​e−2​λ​M\Phi(\lambda,m,n)<\beta\,e^{-2\lambda M}.

Proof.

First moment. By the triangle inequality and ‖δ^j​zj⊤‖F≤R\|\hat{\delta}_{j}z_{j}^{\top}\|_{F}\leq R a.s.,

‖Tw‖F≤∑j∈𝒞pj​‖α​δ^j​zj⊤‖F≤α​R​∑j∈𝒞pja.s.\|T_{w}\|_{F}\;\leq\;\sum_{j\in\mathcal{C}}p_{j}\,\|\alpha\hat{\delta}_{j}z_{j}^{\top}\|_{F}\;\leq\;\alpha R\sum_{j\in\mathcal{C}}p_{j}\quad\text{a.s.}

Taking expectation and applying exchangeability of (pj,𝟏{j∈𝒞})(p_{j},\mathbf{1}\{j\in\mathcal{C}\}) across jj (Lemma 5),

𝔼∥Tw∥F≤αR𝔼[∑j=1npj 1{j∈𝒞}]=αRnβ𝔼[p1∣1∈𝒞].\mathbb{E}\|T_{w}\|_{F}\;\leq\;\alpha R\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{j=1}^{n}p_{j}\,\mathbf{1}\{j\in\mathcal{C}\}\right]=\alpha R\,n\beta\,\mathbb{E}[p_{1}\mid 1\in\mathcal{C}].

By Remark 6, p1=eλ​Ψ1/Q≤eλ​Ψ1​eλ​M/np_{1}=e^{\lambda\Psi_{1}}/Q\leq e^{\lambda\Psi_{1}}\,e^{\lambda M}/n a.s., so

𝔼⁡[p1∣1∈𝒞]≤eλ​Mn​𝔼​[eλ​Ψ1| 1∈𝒞]=eλ​M​Φ𝒞​(λ)n.\mathbb{E}[p_{1}\mid 1\in\mathcal{C}]\;\leq\;\frac{e^{\lambda M}}{n}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[e^{\lambda\Psi_{1}}\,\big|\,1\in\mathcal{C}\right]\;=\;\frac{e^{\lambda M}\,\Phi_{\mathcal{C}}(\lambda)}{n}.

By Lemma 6 Φ𝒞​(λ)≤Φ𝒞¯​(λ)​Φ​(λ,m,n)\Phi_{\mathcal{C}}(\lambda)\leq\Phi_{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}(\lambda)\,\Phi(\lambda,m,n) together with the deterministic bound Φ𝒞¯​(λ)≤eλ​M\Phi_{\bar{\mathcal{C}}}(\lambda)\leq e^{\lambda M} (from Ψ1≤M\Psi_{1}\leq M a.s.),

𝔼⁡[p1∣1∈𝒞]≤e2​λ​M​Φ​(λ,m,n)n,\mathbb{E}[p_{1}\mid 1\in\mathcal{C}]\;\leq\;\frac{e^{2\lambda M}\,\Phi(\lambda,m,n)}{n},

and (7) follows.

Now we can obtain a comparison in worst-case expected bias from each of θ^,θ^p,θ^val\hat{\theta},\hat{\theta}_{p},\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{val}} under additional assumptions.

Assumption 5.

We assume the equivalent of D1 for the empirical covariance of the validation set, i.e. that the minimum eigenvalue is similarly bounded by μ>0\mu>0.

Assumption 6.

Assume the regularity condition that for each output dimension a∈[d]a\in[d], the row εa∈ℝn\varepsilon_{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} of the noise matrix ε\varepsilon satisfies

𝔼[εaεa⊤∣P,Z]⪯σε2In,\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{a}\varepsilon_{a}^{\top}\mid P,Z]\preceq\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}I_{n},

i.e., conditioning on the weights does not inflate the noise’s second moment. This holds at leading order when the weight–noise interaction is benign (for example under sample splitting, i.e. fitting on one subset of training data, then weighting and refitting on the complement).

Lemma 8 (Regret–MSE bridge).

Suppose Assumption 2 holds, the LP diameter L:=supx,x′∈𝒳‖x−x′‖L:=\sup_{x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}}\|x-x^{\prime}\| is finite, and the irreducible noise ε\varepsilon is σε\sigma_{\varepsilon}-sub-Gaussian (so 𝔼​‖ε‖2≤d​σε2\mathbb{E}\|\varepsilon\|^{2}\leq d\,\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}). For any estimator θ\theta independent of the test sample w=(z,c)w=(z,c),

𝔼⁡[Regret⁡(θ)]≤C1​𝔼​‖θ−θ⋆‖F 2+C2.\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Regret}(\theta)]\;\leq\;C_{1}\,\mathbb{E}\,\|\theta-\theta^{\star}\|_{F}^{\,2}\;+\;C_{2}.

where C1=2​L​ω​R2C_{1}=2L\omega R^{2} and C2=8​L​ω​d​σε2C_{2}=8L\omega\,d\,\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}.

Proof.

Write c^:=θ​z\hat{c}:=\theta z, x^:=x⋆​(c^)\hat{x}:=x^{\star}(\hat{c}), x⋆:=x⋆​(c)x^{\star}:=x^{\star}(c), so that c−c^=ε−(θ−θ⋆)​zc-\hat{c}=\varepsilon-(\theta-\theta^{\star})z and ‖c−c^‖≤‖(θ−θ⋆)​z‖+‖ε‖\|c-\hat{c}\|\leq\|(\theta-\theta^{\star})z\|+\|\varepsilon\|.

From ⟨c^,x^⟩≤⟨c^,x⋆⟩\langle\hat{c},\hat{x}\rangle\leq\langle\hat{c},x^{\star}\rangle (optimality of x^\hat{x} at cost c^\hat{c}),

Regret=⟨c−c^,x^−x⋆⟩+⟨c^,x^−x⋆⟩≤‖c−c^‖⋅‖x^−x⋆‖≤L​‖c−c^‖.\mathrm{Regret}=\langle c-\hat{c},\,\hat{x}-x^{\star}\rangle+\langle\hat{c},\,\hat{x}-x^{\star}\rangle\leq\|c-\hat{c}\|\cdot\|\hat{x}-x^{\star}\|\leq L\,\|c-\hat{c}\|.

The bound is vacuously zero when x^=x⋆\hat{x}=x^{\star}.

The event {x^≠x⋆}\{\hat{x}\neq x^{\star}\} implies c^\hat{c} and cc lie in different optimality cones, hence ‖c−c^‖≥πv​(c)\|c-\hat{c}\|\geq\pi_{v}(c). Since πv\pi_{v} is the distance to a fixed closed union of hyperplanes, it is 11-Lipschitz, so

πv​(c)=πv​(θ⋆​z+ε)≥πv​(θ⋆​z)−‖ε‖≥1/ω−‖ε‖.\pi_{v}(c)=\pi_{v}(\theta^{\star}z+\varepsilon)\geq\pi_{v}(\theta^{\star}z)-\|\varepsilon\|\geq 1/\omega-\|\varepsilon\|.

{x^≠x⋆}⊆{∥(θ−θ⋆)z∥+2∥ε∥≥1/ω}.\{\hat{x}\neq x^{\star}\}\subseteq\bigl\{\|(\theta-\theta^{\star})z\|+2\|\varepsilon\|\geq 1/\omega\bigr\}.

Let X:=‖(θ−θ⋆)​z‖+2​‖ε‖X:=\|(\theta-\theta^{\star})z\|+2\|\varepsilon\|. Then by the above calculations

Regret≤L∥c−c^∥ 1{X≥1/ω}≤LX 1{X≥1/ω}≤LωX2,\mathrm{Regret}\leq L\,\|c-\hat{c}\|\,\mathbf{1}\{X\geq 1/\omega\}\leq L\,X\,\mathbf{1}\{X\geq 1/\omega\}\leq L\omega\,X^{2},

using x 1{x≥1/ω}≤ωx2x\,\mathbf{1}\{x\geq 1/\omega\}\leq\omega x^{2} for x≥0x\geq 0. By (a+b)2≤2​a2+2​b2(a+b)^{2}\leq 2a^{2}+2b^{2}, X2≤2​‖(θ−θ⋆)​z‖2+8​‖ε‖2X^{2}\leq 2\,\|(\theta-\theta^{\star})z\|^{2}+8\|\varepsilon\|^{2}.

We use the following standing relationships among the constants, established in Lemma 7:
