Appendix B Additional experiments

B.1 Corruption rate study shortest path

We vary the corruption rate β\beta across [0.1,0.5], observing that there is a similar tradeoff in corruption rate for θ^p\hat{\theta}_{p} vs θ^val\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{val}} as seen in Figure 2. As corruption rate increases, both unweighted and iterative exp. directed suffer in performance, while validation only remains constant. In particular, β=0.3\beta=0.3 appears to be the crossover point. This is to be expected, as once the dataset becomes sufficiently noisy, it is difficult to fit on, regardless of reweighting or not, but we do observe that our method consistently retains lower regret compared to the unweighted ERM. These experiments were run on shortest path problems with fixed parameters over 50 seeds: 4 ×4\times 4 grid, upstream input dimension 30, 400 training points, 100 validation points, 200 test points.

The full table is given below in Table 3

B.2 Validation study shortest path full details

We provide the performance of all methods across varying validation set sizes, not just the unweighted and validation only baselines. We see that RC Weight very slightly outperforms the unweighted baseline in performance particularly at smaller validation sizes, whereas our method excels starting in the medium validation set size range, with a larger margin. Results were obtained on the shortest path setting with 100 seeds on a 4×44\times 4 grid with upstream input dimension 2020, 500500 training points, 200200 test points, and β=0.2\beta=0.2, using the base setting from Table 1.

We also provide the same setting with β=0.3\beta=0.3 for Figure 1, where we demonstrate the crossing over point of Validation Only which is readily apparent at the higher corruption rate.

B.3 Corruption rate study for random LP

We provide a similar study on corruption rate, now with the random LP downstream. The gaps between the reweighting methods are small: Iterative Exp. Directed and SPO Influence Weight (paired p≥0.18p\geq 0.18), and both improve on unweighted ERM by a modest margin that is significant at β=0.3\beta=0.3 (p=0.016p=0.016). Validation Only is constant across β\beta and attains the lowest mean regret at β=0.5\beta=0.5 as much of the data has been corrupted, but the difference to our method is within noise (p=0.42p=0.42); the clean-ERM ceiling shows that the total damage from corruption is small in this setting (0.0250.025 to 0.080.08 regret), which bounds what any reweighting can recover. The SPO+ baselines do not help here: fine-tuning on the validation set is worse than unweighted ERM at every β\beta, and training on the validation set alone is far worse. Results were obtained with upstream input dimension 1010, LP dimension 1010, 2020 constraints, train set size 200200, validation set size 5050, test set size 100100, and 100100 seeds.

B.4 Validation size study for random LP

We provide a similar study on validation set size, but for random LP downstream. Like we have previously observed, the impact of RCIF reweighting is less apparent in this setting (although still present). In particular, it appears that the range of validation set sizes for which the RCIF scoring performs better than unweighted is smaller, which is likely due to the lack of structure in the downstream problem. Results were obtained with upstream input dimension 10, LP dimension 10, 20 constraints, train set size 200, test set size 100, and corruption rate β=0.5\beta=0.5.

B.5 Adversarial noise

Beyond the isotropic Gaussian corruption considered in the main experiments, we also evaluate our method against a more targeted adversary that uses minimum-norm perturbations to flip the optimality cone of corrupted training points. This corruption model is particularly challenging for influence-based methods because it is designed to induce wrong downstream decisions while remaining as close as possible to the clean label.

Construction.

For a corrupted index j∈𝒞j\in\mathcal{C} with clean cost cjc_{j}, let BjB_{j} be the optimal basis for cjc_{j} and let N⁡(Bj)N(B_{j}) denote the corresponding nonbasic set. The minimum ℓ2\ell_{2}-norm perturbation that pushes cjc_{j} across the boundary of Λ⁡(Bj)\Lambda(B_{j}) along nonbasic direction kk has magnitude sk​(cj,Bj)/‖δ⁡(Bj,k)‖s_{k}(c_{j},B_{j})/\|\delta(B_{j},k)\|. The cheapest direction to flip is

kj†=arg⁡mink∈N⁡(Bj)⁡sk​(cj,Bj)‖δ⁡(Bj,k)‖.k^{\dagger}_{j}\;=\;\arg\min_{k\in N(B_{j})}\,\frac{s_{k}(c_{j},B_{j})}{\|\delta(B_{j},k)\|}.

Given a budget ρ>0\rho>0, the adversarial corruption is

c~j=cj−αj​δ⁡(Bj,kj†)‖δ⁡(Bj,kj†)‖,αj=min⁡(ρ,(1+ε)​skj†​(cj,Bj)‖δ⁡(Bj,kj†)‖),\tilde{c}_{j}\;=\;c_{j}-\alpha_{j}\,\frac{\delta(B_{j},k^{\dagger}_{j})}{\|\delta(B_{j},k^{\dagger}_{j})\|},\qquad\alpha_{j}=\min\!\left(\rho,\;\frac{(1+\varepsilon)\,s_{k^{\dagger}_{j}}(c_{j},B_{j})}{\|\delta(B_{j},k^{\dagger}_{j})\|}\right),

with a small slack ε>0\varepsilon>0 to ensure the perturbation strictly crosses the boundary when budget allows, which is similar to the directional attack in Assumption D4, but with a variable magnitude. If ρ\rho is insufficient to flip any direction, we use the full budget along the cheapest flip direction without crossing.

Note that the perturbation magnitude is minimal rather than fixed: the adversary uses just enough perturbation to cross a cone boundary, producing small residuals at the clean ERM estimator and weak first-order influence signals.

Empirical observations.

Under cone-flipping corruption, all methods including ours perform comparably to unweighted ERM, with no method showing a significant improvement over unweighted (Table 8), perhaps due to the magnitude of the corruption being small so they perform similarly to unweighted. Diagnostic analysis confirms that the RCIF score does carry information distinguishing corrupted from clean points: the mean score over corrupted indices is consistently more negative than over clean indices but the separation is insufficient for reliable detection. We attribute this to a fundamental property of first-order influence methods: the influence of a training point scales with its perturbation magnitude, and minimum-norm adversarial corruption is designed precisely to minimize this signal. Methods based on residual magnitude or influence function approximations are therefore inherently limited against such adversaries, and we expect that defenses against cone-flipping corruption require either second-order influence information or outlier-detection such as Diakonikolas et al. [2019]. Results were obtained with both random LP and shortest path problems. For random LP, settings were upstream input dimension 10, LP dimension 10, 20 constraints, train set size 200, test set size 100, validation set size 50, β=0.3\beta=0.3, ρ=0.3\rho=0.3. For shortest path settings: grid 5 ×\times 5, upstream input dimension 30, train set size 300, test set size 200, validation set size 100, β=0.3\beta=0.3, ρ=0.05\rho=0.05. ρ\rho is much smaller for shortest path because the optimality cones appear to be narrower, and thus require less perturbation to flip.

B.5.1 Adversarial noise with fixed magnitude and robust regression

Residual-based robust regression is the natural alternative to reweighting when training labels are corrupted, so we compare against two standard instances: Huber regression (threshold 1.351.35, fit per output coordinate) and iteratively trimmed least squares (three rounds, each refitting after discarding the training points with the largest residual norms). Both are fit on the same train-plus-validation pool as unweighted ERM. For trimmed ERM we set the trim fraction equal to the true corruption rate β\beta, which is an oracle choice that favors the baseline. We evaluate under two corruption models of the same magnitude scale: the isotropic Gaussian corruption of the main experiments and the directional corruption of Assumption (D4), in which each corrupted label is shifted by a fixed amount α\alpha along the most fragile direction of its own optimality cone. This is the same adversarial noise direction as Section B.5 but with a fixed magnitude, not minimal. Both are run on the shortest-path problem (4×44\times 4 grid, input dimension 2020, 400/100/200400/100/200 train/validation/test points, 5050 seeds), with β=0.2\beta=0.2 for the Gaussian setting and β=0.4\beta=0.4, α=1.5\alpha=1.5 for the directional setting. Table 9 reports the results under various types of noise.

Under isotropic Gaussian corruption the robust methods are strong, and trimmed ERM is the best method in every column: it attains 0.8544±0.01410.8544\pm 0.0141 against 0.9085±0.01640.9085\pm 0.0164 for Iterative Exp. Directed and 0.9600±0.01580.9600\pm 0.0158 for unweighted ERM, and it also improves on our method similarly for random LP (paired Wilcoxon p<0.001p<0.001 in each case) while Huber loss is consistent but shows the greatest gains under random LPs. We note that this is the regime these methods are designed for, and furthermore these methods have been given the corruption rate, an advantage our method nor any other method receives. Gaussian corruption of scale 22 produces residuals that are large relative to the label noise, so a corrupted point is visible in residual norm at the unweighted fit, and trimming at the true rate removes most of them; Huber regression down-weights the same points more gently and lands between unweighted ERM and our method on the shortest-path settings (0.9266±0.01630.9266\pm 0.0163).

Under directional corruption the ordering reverses. The shift α=1.5\alpha=1.5 is small relative to the label noise and does not stand out in residual norm, but it is aimed at the fragile direction of the cone and flips the optimal decision of every corrupted point. Trimmed ERM now discards clean points as often as corrupted ones and reaches 0.8977±0.01580.8977\pm 0.0158, worse than unweighted ERM (0.8591±0.01640.8591\pm 0.0164) on 84%84\% of seeds (p<0.001p<0.001); Huber reaches 0.8730±0.01560.8730\pm 0.0156, also worse than unweighted ERM (p<0.001p<0.001). Iterative Exp. Directed is better at 0.8509±0.01640.8509\pm 0.0164, improving on unweighted ERM (p=0.036p=0.036) and on both robust baselines (p<0.001p<0.001 for each). The total damage is small in this setting (clean ERM attains 0.8257±0.01520.8257\pm 0.0152), which compresses all gaps, but the sign of the effect is what matters: the robust losses lose ground precisely when the corruption is decision-targeted rather than magnitude-visible.

The two experiments isolate different notions of robustness. Residual-based methods are robust to corruption magnitude and require that corrupted labels be outliers in the regression sense, together with a well-specified model and, for trimming, knowledge of the corruption rate and noise type. RCIF reweighting is robust to decision-targeted corruption: it scores a training point by its first-order effect on the reduced-cost margins at the clean validation points, which responds to where a label pushes the downstream decision rather than to how far it moves the label, and it requires neither the corruption rate nor magnitude-visible residuals. We regard the two approaches as complementary, and combining RCIF scores with a robust training loss is a natural direction for future work.

B.6 Degeneracy

Note that shortest-path and combinatorial problems generally violate primal nondegeneracy. For LPs with generic continuous bb and full-row-rank AA (such as our random-LP setting, or pricing/portfolio-style problems with continuous coefficients), degeneracy is a measure-zero event, so the assumption holds almost surely. More importantly, the assumption serves the theory rather than the algorithm: the method still functions and applies to degenerate problems, at the cost of some conservatism.

The algorithm itself never uses nondegeneracy: it solves one LP per validation point under the predicted cost, takes whichever optimal basis the solver returns, and determines correctness via the cone test sk​(cv,Bv)≥0∀k∈N⁡(Bv)s_{k}(c_{v},B_{v})\geq 0\ \ \forall k\in N(B_{v}), which is well defined under degeneracy. The cost of degeneracy is conservatism: the containment Λ⁡(Bv)⊆𝒩⁡(x∗​(c^v))\Lambda(B_{v})\subseteq\mathcal{N}(x^{*}(\hat{c}_{v})) becomes strict, so the algorithm may mark a correct decision as incorrect when cvc_{v} certifies the same vertex through a different basis, and the computed margin is a lower bound on the true decision margin. We note that (i) the correctness certificate never certifies a truly suboptimal point; and (ii) for the directed variant, such a misclassification is harmless at the point in question, because the violated directions there are all degenerate pivots. Its cost is signal efficiency, since part of the validation signal is spent on basis bookkeeping rather than on actual decisions. Empirically, our gains are largest on shortest path, which we take as evidence that the conservative signal remains strong where the assumption fails

B.7 Experimental details

B.7.1 Hardware and software

All experiments were conducted on a personal laptop equipped with an Intel i7 CPU, 16GB RAM, and no dedicated GPU. Implementation required standard Python packages such as PyTorch, scikit-learn, as well as Gurobipy and Gurobi software for the optimization aspects. Each seed (which involves all baselines and optimization calls) runs in approximately 4 minutes. Code for reproducing our experiments is available at: https://github.com/william-zhang64/Reduced-Cost-Influence-Functions.

B.7.2 Parameter and baseline settings

Throughout the experiments, we kept λ\lambda fixed at 0.05. The values λ=0.05\lambda=0.05 and τ=5\tau=5 were selected during preliminary experimentation across a grid of values {0.01,0.05,0.1,0.5}\{0.01,0.05,0.1,0.5\} and {3,5,10}\{3,5,10\} respectively, with a plateau in performance for λ∈{0.05,0.1}\lambda\in\{0.05,0.1\}. Qualitatively, larger λ\lambda produced overly extreme weights and degraded test regret, consistent with overfitting the small clean validation set, while smaller λ\lambda left the weights too close to uniform to counteract the corruption. The number of iterations behaves similarly: beyond roughly τ=5\tau=5 we observed a plateau in performance. Given that the pair (λ,τ)=(0.05,5)(\lambda,\tau)=(0.05,5) was used across the settings in the paper for strong performance, this suggests these values serve as reasonable defaults. Note that the weights were normalized such that unweighted had each weight = 1.0, so the total weights sum to nn rather than 1, which does not substantively affect any properties of the algorithm. Similarly, the ϕ\phi parameter for the Directed method was also fixed to 0.05, for similar reasons. We used τ=5\tau=5 iterations across the experiments for the Iterative Exp. Directed method. For SPO influence, we set the number of iterations to 5 as well, with learning rate of 0.01. For SPO+ Val Only we run full-batch subgradient descent on the SPO+ loss over the validation set for 100 epochs with normalized subgradients and diminishing step size 0.5/t+10.5/\sqrt{t+1}, initialized at the validation-only least-squares fit, and keep the iterate with the lowest SPO+ objective. SPO+ Finetune uses the same procedure initialized at the unweighted least-squares fit on the train-plus-validation pool, with 30 epochs and step size 0.1/t+10.1/\sqrt{t+1}. Huber regression uses threshold 1.35 and is fit per output coordinate on the train-plus-validation pool, and trimmed ERM runs three rounds, each refitting after discarding the fraction β\beta of training points with the largest residual norms. For the random LP data-generating process, we used standard normal distribution for features. For the isotropic noise, we used a covariance matrix of 4ℐd\mathcal{I}_{d} and for the directional noise with fixed magnitude we used α=1.5\alpha=1.5. For the neural network, we used hidden layer of size 8, with learning rate 1e-3.

B.7.3 Computational cost

Each iteration of RCIF reweighting solves the downstream LP once at each of the mm validation points, computes the influence functions of the nn training points, and refits the predictor by weighted least squares. The LP is never differentiated through and is not solved at training points. For the linear predictor with squared loss the influence has the closed form of Lemma 1: the Hessian is 2​Id⊗Σ^2I_{d}\otimes\hat{\Sigma}, so one q×qq\times q factorization is shared by all training and validation points. Forming Σ^\hat{\Sigma}, its inverse, and the residuals rj=θ^​zj−c~jr_{j}=\hat{\theta}z_{j}-\tilde{c}_{j} costs O⁡(n​q​(q+d)+q3)O(nq(q+d)+q^{3}) per iteration. At a validation point vv with direction δk\delta_{k}, the scores of all nn training points are the elementwise product of δk⊤​rj\delta_{k}^{\top}r_{j}, an n×dn\times d matrix-vector product, and κ⁡(zv,zj)=zj⊤​Σ^−1​zv\kappa(z_{v},z_{j})=z_{j}^{\top}\hat{\Sigma}^{-1}z_{v}, an n×qn\times q one, so scoring over the validation set costs O⁡(m​n​(q+d))O(mn(q+d)); the weighted least-squares refit on the n+mn+m points is absorbed into the same terms. The LP solves and basis information cost O⁡(m​TLP)O(m\,T_{\mathrm{LP}}) per iteration, where TLPT_{\mathrm{LP}} is the cost of one simplex solve, and the iterative variant repeats all of this τ\tau times. In practice the τ​m\tau m LP solves dominate: on a laptop CPU with Gurobi, in the shortest-path setting of Table 1 (n=400n=400, m=100m=100), one scoring round takes about 0.50.5 s and the complete Iterative Exp. Directed fit with τ=5\tau=5 about 22 s.

B.7.4 SPO Influence

We adapt the influence-based reweighting framework of Ren et al. [2018] to the predict-then-optimize setting by substituting the SPO+ surrogate loss [Elmachtoub and Grigas, 2022] for validation MSE. This isolates the contribution of LP cone geometry in our scoring from the general benefit of influence-based reweighting on a downstream-aware loss.

For predicted cost c^v=fθ^​(zv)\hat{c}_{v}=f_{\hat{\theta}}(z_{v}) and true cost cvc_{v}, SPO+ is a convex upper bound on regret with subgradient

g⁡(c^v,cv)= 2​(x∗​(cv)−x∗​(2​c^v−cv)),g(\hat{c}_{v},c_{v})\;=\;2\big(x^{*}(c_{v})-x^{*}(2\hat{c}_{v}-c_{v})\big),

where x∗​(c)=arg⁡minx∈𝒳​c⊤​xx^{*}(c)=\arg\min_{x\in\mathcal{X}}c^{\top}x. Composing with the influence function ℐθ^​(wj)\mathcal{I}_{\hat{\theta}}(w_{j}) gives the per-training-point sensitivity of validation loss:

ΣjSPO+=1m​∑wv∈𝒱g​(c^v,cv)⊤​∇θfθ^​(zv)​ℐθ^​(wj).\Sigma^{\text{SPO+}}_{j}\;=\;\frac{1}{m}\sum_{w_{v}\in\mathcal{V}}g(\hat{c}_{v},c_{v})^{\top}\,\nabla_{\theta}f_{\hat{\theta}}(z_{v})\,\mathcal{I}_{\hat{\theta}}(w_{j}).

Starting from uniform weights pj(0)=1p^{(0)}_{j}=1, we iteratively update

pj(t+1)←max⁡(0,pj(t)−ξ​ΣjSPO+|θ^(t)),p^{(t+1)}_{j}\;\leftarrow\;\max\!\big(0,\;p^{(t)}_{j}-\xi\,\Sigma^{\text{SPO+}}_{j}\big|_{\hat{\theta}^{(t)}}\big),

normalize so that ∑jpj(t+1)=n\sum_{j}p^{(t+1)}_{j}=n, and refit θ^(t+1)\hat{\theta}^{(t+1)} via weighted ERM. We use ξ=0.01\xi=0.01 and run for τ=5\tau=5 iterations.

This baseline matches RCIF in data usage and influence machinery; the methods differ only in the projection direction for the prediction shift: g⁡(c^v,cv)g(\hat{c}_{v},c_{v}) for SPO+ versus the simplex direction δ⁡(Bv,k)\delta(B_{v},k) for RCIF.
